title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Nicholas Galitzine and Bill Skarsgard in Peter Berg’s Technically Impressive, Emotionally Hollow Netflix War Drama
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 7:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Mosquito Bowl' Kane Skennar / Netflix The Mosquito Bowl , Peter Berg ’s new World War II drama for Netflix, sets the tone right away with a famous Herbert Hoover quote. “Older men declare war,” it goes. “But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war.” It is a statement eternal in its truth and devastating in its poignancy, one well worth keeping in mind any time the specter of battle is raised. It is also, you may have noticed, the theme of more or less every single war movie ever made. It would take some really sharp and distinctive execution to make it feel fresh again — and as admirable as The Mosquito Bowl often is in its craft, its storytelling falls well short of that bar. Related Stories Movies Friday Night Fights: Peter Berg Returns to Football ... and War Movies Peter Berg's Netflix War Movie 'The Mosquito Bowl' to Premiere at AFI Fest (Exclusive) The Mosquito Bowl The Bottom Line Looks good but says little. Venue: AFI Fest Release date: Friday, Oct. 30 Cast: Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgard, Ray Nicholson, Tom Francis Director: Peter Berg Screenwriters: Peter Berg, Mark L. Smith Rated R, 2 hours 6 minutes The premise, at least, had potential. Adapted from the book of the same title by Buzz Bissinger (whose Friday Night Lights also spawned a Berg film), The Mosquito Bowl leads up to a legendary football game played between two Marine divisions while stationed at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve in 1944. One would expect the sports angle to add a welcome new spin on the usual war-drama storylines — and it does, though not nearly as much as you’re probably guessing, given how little of the 126-minute run time the match actually takes up. Its leads are a quartet of elite college football players who’ve joined the Marines after the 1941 bombing of Pearl Harbor, and all are played by hot rising stars du jour: the ubiquitous but apparently un – typecast – able Nicholas Galitzine as thoughtful Brown alum John McLaughry; Ray Nicholson as charming Purdue alum turned promising NFL draftee Tony Butkovich; Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgard as anxious David Schreiner and wild Bob Bauman, both graduates of University of Wisconsin (though only David maintains a grudge against Tony for beating them in a pivotal game). But if that Hoover epigraph suggests a well-trod path, the rest of the film confirms it has no intention of straying from it. The central themes are all ones you could guess based on the logline alone. War forges unbreakable bonds of brotherhood. War makes men out of boys, but destroys their minds and bodies in the process. War is hell, as opposed to football, which represents youthful idealism, except that football is also a little bit like war if you think about it: “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in the history of football,” one character declares. The Mosquito Bowl ’s great saving grace — the thing that might nevertheless make it worthwhile for people who simply enjoy war movies — are its technical elements. (Well, maybe aside from the dull gray-brown-blue color palette that seems to aim for “serious and gritty” and lands right back at “produced by Netflix.”) Combat sequences, set in the Pacific theater and filmed in Australia, look expansive and authentic, weaving around hundreds of soldiers running and shouting and shooting at once. Berg, working with DP Jacques Jouffret, favors close shots that force us to experience battle much like our heroes do, as confusing, terrifying bursts of mayhem. Pinned in place by the machine guns we hear thundering all around, we watch in horror as a friend gets struck down by a bullet mid-conversation, or flamethrowers wave wildly in the periphery. But that’s often all we get. Other soldiers, friendlies and enemies alike, are glimpsed through trees or plumes of smoke. Updates get passed around like rumors. What lurks over the next ridge or the next nightfall is anyone’s guess. Given that commitment to their perspective, I suppose you could argue that these scenes dragging on for quite a while is part of the idea, too: The guys who’d previously hoped to be home in time for the Fourth of July — of 1942 — are learning the hard way that fighting rarely goes so quick or easy. But as the minutes stretch on, it starts to seem that The Mosquito Bowl is primarily interested in showing off how skilled Berg and his team are at producing action set pieces, be they ones of battle or boot camp or football, and only secondarily interested in its plot or characters. This impression is not diminished by a script, from Berg and Mark L. Smith, that barely bothers to build any connective tissue between said set pieces. Even the titular Mosquito Bowl finally arrives with almost no build-up at all. No sooner has one Marine complained about low morale than a sergeant has assigned two others to organize a football game; no sooner has that order gone out than we’re watching them line up to play it. Logically, the necessary pieces are all accounted for; it’s not as if we need to watch Bob and David recruiting teammates to surmise that that must have happened at some point. But in its constant rush to get to the good stuff, The Mosquito Bowl keeps shortchanging the emotional beats required to make them land. Personalities are sketched only in the margins, mostly via brief snippets of chatter between rounds of gunfire. Character development happens offscreen, or possibly doesn’t exist at all — it’s hard to tell if anyone’s changing when everyone’s so vaguely conceived to begin with. The big ideas we’re meant to take to heart are reduced to disingenuous platitudes. While The Mosquito Bowl does not completely ignore the nastier undercurrents of the military culture and mindset, it’s so invested in the idea of wartime service as an act of noble self-sacrifice that it refuses to engage with them directly. So even as Bob announces in boot camp that “This recruit is here to learn how to kill Japanese people, sir!” the film never stops to reexamine his eagerness or his motives. It introduces such details only to gloss by them completely on the way to a straightforwardly heroic ending. This refusal to look directly at the shadows is all the more aggravating given how often The Mosquito Bowl pats itself on the back for being clear-eyed. In quieter moments, the film zooms out into a placid view of the globe from space, or zooms into bittersweet details like a seagull walking along a corpse-strewn beach — reminders to maintain a sense of perspective about our place in this vast and indifferent universe. In moments of grand emotion, it often freezes into black-and-white snapshots (sometimes pulled from actual archives) to emphasize that what we’re watching really happened. But in the rest of its run time, it forgets that just because something is true doesn’t mean you can’t make it ring false. title: Tony Dokoupil Has a Question: Will You Watch His New Podcast? (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Great Question' with Tony Dokoupil. CBS News Tony Dokoupil is launching a podcast, and if you happen to watch the video version and look very, very closely, there’s a chance you could spot Salvador Dali’s phone number. Dokoupil, the anchor of the CBS Evening News , is now almost 11 months into the job, and to hear him explain it, he is just beginning to find his rhythm and footing in the high-profile role. So that makes for an opportune moment to expand the Evening News to digital platforms with a wholly original podcast extension: Great Question with Tony Dokoupil . It will be available in video form (on YouTube and all the other podcast platforms), shot in his office, alongside audio versions. “You’re going to get to see my dad’s mugshot on the shelf behind me [he was arrested for smuggling marijuana in 1992], and my great uncle’s pioneering gay advocacy journal that he came out with called Michael’s Thing on the shelf behind me, and all my old Newsweek covers and a bunch of books I like,” Dokoupil says, noting all the paraphernalia, before landing on his favorite: “I rescued a Rolodex from the dump when Newsweek was on the brink of folding.” And yes, it has Dali’s phone number. Great Question will be built off of the foundation of the Evening News , but it will also be its own thing. The premise? Twice per week, on Mondays and Wednesdays, Dokoupil will focus on one “great question,” looking to journalists or experts to help answer it. “When I think of the Evening News , I think of our beat as being the story of America one day at a time, which is why I always have that sign off, ‘that’s another day in America,’ and even though we have this amazing team and these global resources and we put out a jam-packed show, there are still things we couldn’t get to the bottom of, and so every day starts with new questions,” Dokoupil explains. “Over the course of a week, there’ll be things that we didn’t get to or that are lingering, and the hope of the podcast is you’ll be able to distill that into the biggest, most urgent, most pressing, most important, or just most interesting question, and then you try to match that to a guest.” Watch the trailer: Among those guests will be author and podcast host Malcolm Gladwell to discuss whether America needs more police and 60 Minutes contributor Gianna Toboni talking about the death penalty. Episodes will focus on why America kids seem so bad at math, if gambling apps are trying to addict us, and other tough or interesting questions. The show “is an effort to capture that curiosity and have a format where I’m asking a question that is genuinely occurring to me in the moment that I genuinely want to know the answer to, and I don’t know what’s going to happen next,” he says. But for Dokoupil the show is also a chance to show his voice, and to help a digitally-native audience that might not watch the Evening News understand who he is as a journalist and as a person. “There are people who watch traditional TV and they love it, they love the product, they grew up with it, they’re still into it, and that’s a great audience,” Dokoupil says. “There’s another group of people who are more online who genuinely believe that people on TV are just getting things fed into their earpiece, and they’re basically robots with hair pieces on. That is a real meaningful part of the population.” “And I think part of the advantage of a podcast is when you’ve been around as long as I have, and you have stories from the field and the things you’ve learned, giving people an opportunity to hear you talk at length with somebody else who knows a lot, who’s been around, and have a genuine conversation — it just exposes new people to who you are as a journalist,” he continues. “What excites you? What interests you? And it deepens that one-on-one relationship, which is what works on television, and is also I think what works in podcasts .” Dokoupil hopes that it gives viewers a little slice of who he is outside of those 30 minutes every weekday, and outside of other things he does for CBS, like last week’s town hall with Vice President JD Vance, or next month’s midterm election coverage, which he will co-anchor with Norah O’Donnell. And it comes as he says he has finally found his footing at the Evening News . “At the beginning, I felt like Mr. Smith Goes to Washington , I was naively walking into this new neighborhood, and it took me a little while to realize all the ways in which it’s not the morning show,” he recalls, adding that “a lot of people didn’t know my work or who I was. “Different people are watching, and they have different ideas about what works, and everything I think flows from that.” he adds. “But now, 10 months in, I understand it, I love it.” A big part of that has been finding his voice in the anchor chair, and refining the stories the show covers. “I think when we launched, we were pretty heavy on politics. And politics are important, we cover it every night, sometimes with two beats, sometimes with even more, but it’s not everything,” he says. “And I think we’ve found a mix that’s right for us. I also think the sound of the show has changed in a way that’s been great. I write or revise every single word that comes out of my mouth… I think now people can tell when they’re hearing it, it’s really me.” And now Great Question will, hopefully CBS News thinks, bring that voice to new places, in a digital expansion that is unusual for an evening news anchor. “I believe in the form. I like podcasts myself, so there’s that,” Dokoupil says. “But also, you know, I’ve been doing the Evening News for 10 months now, almost a year, we’re in a good rhythm with the show, we like the direction of the show, we feel the momentum, and we realize we had the resources and the space to fit a podcast in, and it would give us the opportunity to pursue the longer questions and answers that are often the most exciting part of journalism.” THR

title: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I’ Star Morgana Robinson on Sacha Baron Cohen Not Letting Her Break Character as ‘Me Julie’ and Why Film Doesn’t Mock Working Class
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 7:00am PT ‘Ali G: Who Iz I’ Star Morgana Robinson on Sacha Baron Cohen Not Letting Her Break Character as ‘Me Julie’ and Why Film Doesn’t Mock Working Class By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc 30 minutes ago Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones Support ‘Normal People’ Author Sally Rooney After U.K. Book Ban: She’s a ‘Writer, Not a Terrorist’ 2 days ago The Beatles Immersive Experience, Featuring Sets and Props From Sam Mendes’ Biopics, Set for Liverpool 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Variety via Getty Images After more than a decade out of the limelight and away from his wardrobe of high-visibility, low-practicality clothing, Sacha Baron Cohen ‘s Ali G is back with his first film in almost 25 years. This time, alongside the satirical would-be bad boy himself leading “Ali G: Who Iz I” comes his long-suffering girlfriend Julie (constantly referred to by Ali as “Me Julie”). Played by British comic and impressionist Morgana Robinson, Julie is seen in the trailer to the film — released Oct. 23 by Amazon MGM — heavily pregnant while Ali first explains to a doctor that her bump is “probably wind or a big poo” and later with him as, when asked what type of father he wants to be, he replies “absent.” Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ For Middleton, who played Pippa Middleton in “The Windsors,” the experience making “Ali G: Who Iz I” was the most insane she’s ever had, one that required her, on the insistence of Cohen, to stay in character off set. “He was training me like Rocky,” she says. But for all the silliness of the film (Morgana claims it’s half-silly — ”laugh-out loud funny, but with a message”), “Ali G: Who Iz I” has also come under significant fire, accused of using outdated racist stereotypes and mocking the working class. In the U.K., there have also been calls for cinemas to boycott the film. Popular on Variety Speaking to Variety , a wildly entertaining Morgana claims that Julie — who she describes as “the heart of the film” — is much more than what’s been seen in the trailer, adding that the “Who Iz I” actually takes aim at Ali G’s out-of-date views and attitude. But she also laughs about the shock and surprise of finding people in America who didn’t know Ali G and could be duped by the joke and reveals the real — and painful — struggles of trying not to laugh during each scene, because “there is no take two.” How’s the “Ali G: Who Iz I” press tour been? I’m in a bowl of jelly, to be honest. It is a bit knee-knocky. It’s on a rather grand scale, but it’s been amazing, especially on the red carpet and turning up in character. Most carpets are quite serious affairs with serious questions. Was turning up as Julie and, I guess, ad lobbing a bit quite fun? I find it a bit of a comfort. It’s like a very solid bra. I feel supported and not so exposed. They can look a bit serious, can’t they? And if you look a bit silly, it’s fine. So how silly is this film? It’s half-silly. It gets less silly as you go on. But it’s got all the feels. It’s outrageous. It’s very funny. It’s terrifying. It’s uncomfortable. It’s heartbreaking. It’s confusing. But it’s laugh out loud funny, but with a message. We haven’t had Ali G on screens for a very long time. How does he rank to the Ali G of old? He hasn’t changed particularly much, apart from you know his beard’s a bit longer. But how does he sit into today’s society? I think that’s sort of the reason they made this —what happens when you take a very dated character and drop him in into today’s society, into the world that we live in today that’s a very different place. Does he manage to survive that? I might let you wait and see. But what I will say is that I think a lot of questions have been asked, and I think they get answers. So how did how did this film find you? How did you become Julie? There was a very rigorous, full-on casting situation, and there were waves of auditions. There was like the first wave of auditions was a sort of like, “Hi, can you come in and have an improv with Sasha? Can you be funny? Can you go toe to toe with him? Can you hold your own?” And then the second, once you’ve passed that, was, “We throw you into the jaws of a shark with a with a real interview with a real person. Can you be believable?” I guess what they were looking for was a balance between someone who could be funny, but also someone who you know could feel real. Otherwise, I guess they don’t have a film. But I think it took them about a year to cast. This film took us all by surprise when it was announced. So much must have been done in secret. Oh yeah, I like the word ‘clandestine.’ It’s an odd it’s an odd fish, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve never done anything like this with real people. It was was crazy. Sometimes we were in the desert in Palm Springs. We stayed in these random hotels, all of us, but no one knew what we were doing there. So it was all sort of cloak and dagger and lying about what we were doing. You’d be doing makeup in your hotel room, and some days I’d come back and I’d have a bob and I’d be not pregnant. Then the next morning, I’d be eight months pregnant, walking out the lobby. Then I’d be in the bar having a glass of wine. And the concierge was just so confused. Previous mockumentaries from Sasha, whether with Ali G or Borat or Bruno, have all relied on people not understanding that it’s a joke. But I’d be surprised if there’s anyone now who doesn’t know. Was it all scripted or were you actually meeting real people who had no idea that this was a joke? Every single person, apart from me and him and the guy who plays his dad, are all real people. It think Borat is well known in America, but Ali G isn’t. But I think the people on the team scouted for people, and they had to pass a sort of certain test of who they know and what they know. That must be quite some scouting. I’m really surprised that someone who’s not been cut off from the world for the last 20 years wouldn’t just see Ali G and know that a joke was coming a mile off. Was it a surprise to you that some people out there were still duped by it? The whole thing is ridiculous. The whole thing is shocking and surprising. I don’t know where to begin. But the script was a constantly evolving thing. It wasn’t like, “Here is the script. You may read it.” It was like, “Here it is and it’s different from yesterday.” So you’re in your room waiting to come on set and 10 minutes before someone runs in going, “Hey Morgana, this has totally changed.” You’re like, “This is chaos. This is ludicrous. They’re never going to believe this. We can’t pull this off. This is impossible.” And I don’t know what happens, but [Cohen] sort of hypnotizes people. it’s like a magic trick. Morgan Robinson. Photo: Lou Rolley Did you struggle not to laugh? Because obviously you can’t start again. You literally have to stay in character or the whole thing’s ruined, right? There’s no take two. So that actually stops you from laughing a lot of the time. I did corpse twice in the entirety of filming. One was when I had to peel a banana with my toes, and the other one was something that happens later, but I don’t want to spoil it. So I did it twice, but I sort of managed to look away and stifle it. I bit so hard on my cheek. That’s one way of doing it. You can sometimes turn it into a cough. Or it can come out as a sort of twitch. But yes, it’s very hard. And after each scene, are you and Sasha able to have a laugh or do you stay in character? He will not let you break character. So we’re in character for eight hours. It’s exhausting. Normally, when you’re acting, you’re like, that was a very big take, is it lunch break? But here you’re eating lunch in character or whatever you’re doing because they’re watching. It’s wild. I remember when we first started filming, I hadn’t seen Sasha since the audition and I got to the lot to do the first rehearsals and talk and read the script. I was like, “Oh, hi Sasha, it’s Morgana, I haven’t seen you for six months.” And he’s like, “In character! All day I want you in character! I never want to hear you speaking as Morgana! It’s always me Julie!” Then he’d march me down to the mall and be like, “Go and have an argument with some people and buy some socks and then come back and then call up your mother and have a conversation as me Julie and eat that bento box as me Julie. How would she use chopsticks?” He’s mad. So you were Julie constantly, if there was a camera on you or not? He was training me like Rocky. All day long, running up and down those steps, all sweaty. How then did it feel then at the end of all that to finally put Julie to bed? I think I lost my marbles a little bit for a while, but I think I found them again. I think it’s sort of like sort of slow release PTSD. I can’t believe we fucking did that. I cannot believe that. I mean.. so I get kidnapped. What? Yeah, I get kidnapped. That’s an actual thing. That’s not even the bad bit. That’s just in the second act. I get kidnapped. But more happens. What can you say? I get my minge out. You’ll probably have to change that because no one knows what a minge is in America. So all these years, I’ve been doing these cute little cult things, like Vic and Bob, and no one’s watched it. Really, all you need to do is just go to Hollywood and get your fanny out. You know, I’m 44. I’ve got to pay the mortgage. The last major thing that Sasha did was Borat 2, which obviously has that scene in a hotel room with Maria Bakalova and Rudy Giuliani. Does it reach those levels? Yes, indeed. But with well-known individuals who are going to be made to feel ashamed of their actions afterwards? No, they’re not politicians. Not in my scenes anyway. When the first trailer came out, there was a lot of noise – some good, some bad. There were quite a few negative comments with regards to the scenes with Julie, with a lot of people saying it was mocking working class women and was quite derogatory. What did you think when you know saw those comments? I found it difficult. So I just stopped reading them entirely. People have their opinions, and that’s absolutely fine. I am a character actress and I play all sorts of people. I play every class, everything and so I feel like that’s what my job is. But think the hard things to read online was when they got really nasty. I get it. But in terms of those claims about the film mocking the working class, is that something that you would remotely agree with? I think she’s a well thought out character. She’s got heart. She’s got soul. She cares very much for her baby. She’s got amazing morals. She loves her family to pieces. She would die for them, as you will see. It’s not just one note. There’s more to her than what you see in the trailer. The film is much more layered. I think they probably designed the trailer a little bit to get people talking. You said that the story is about dropping Ali G, this outdated character, in today’s world. There have also been accusations about him being this tired racist caricature. But it sounds like that’s actually part of the film — is that the case? It’s sort of all about that, really. How’s Sasha to work with? He’s kind of like a giant kid who’s had too much sugarish. Sometimes it’s like trying to wrangle a hurricane. It’s chaos, but in a wonderful way and I think that shows in the work he makes. It’s just not normal, but it’s exciting, you know, and it’s interesting, and exhilarating and also terrifying. All those things. There’s so much adrenaline going around in your in your body. That’s his gift to you. I always felt like in today’s world of social media and everybody knowing everything because it’s all been videoed and posted everywhere, you just couldn’t get away with this kind of stuff anymore. But the fact that they were able to find people that had no idea and keep that joke going is phenomenal. I know it’s crazy. I think this will probably be the last one. ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work Loading comments...

title: Banijay Entertainment’s Frédéric Balmary on U.S. Ambitions, Netflix and the Battle for IP: It’s ‘One of Our Big Fights’
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:56am PT Banijay Entertainment’s Frédéric Balmary on U.S. Ambitions, Netflix and the Battle for IP: It’s ‘One of Our Big Fights’ By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest ‘Galileo,’ Toplining Elio Germano, Boarded by Fandango, Kicking Off Sales at Rome’s MIA Market (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Sebastian Koch, Toni Servillo Set for Oscar Winner Gabriele Salvatores’ Chess-World Noir ‘The Lüneburg Variation’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mary Sullivan Fresh off its merger, the Banijay /All3Media behemoth, now known as Banijay Entertainment, is eyeing an expansion into U.S. scripted production as Netflix looks to ramp up its slate of American hits amid a major shake-up of its content leadership. Speaking at Rome’s MIA Market, Banijay Entertainment chief business officer Frédéric Balmary said in an interview with Variety that the group, which ranks as the world’s largest independent studio, looks to capitalize on Netflix’s renewed focus on U.S. programming, while continuing to grow its English-language scripted business, bolstered by the merger with All3Media, and its roster of talent including George Kay and Sam Mendes. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Balmary also discussed the growing global appetite for European dramas, the U.K.’s role as a bridge between Hollywood and Europe, and the financial pressures facing U.S. studios and streamers. He stressed the importance of retaining IP, echoing CEO Marco Bassetti’s call for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade. “Retaining IP is really one of our big fights at the moment,” Balmary said. Popular on Variety Talk to me about the ongoing growth in English-language dramas output at Banijay. Well, the English language market is certainly growing, and that was also one of the rationales of the merger deal between All3Media and Banijay. At Banijay we were already growing in the U.K. scripted market with a few acquisition we’ve done in past years, like The Forge Entertainment and the other British companies we invest in. But All3 has incredible talents in the scripted sphere, from [“Lupin’ creator] George Kay to Sam Mendes, to many others. We’ve always said that our business is based on talent and IP, and the growing English market is really where we want to be, in order to follow the market. Not only in production, also in distribution. Marco Bassetti recently hinted to an expansion in the U.S. scripted space. Can you tell me more? We are already there, but not as a studio. We’ve done the “Ripley” series and these kinds of things, though more on the packaging side. Today it’s really a growing area. From its last earnings call, it’s clear that Netflix is looking for more U.S. hits. I think that was part of Marco’s vision in saying maybe we will also follow that growth area and be more active in that space in the U.S. How do you see the prospects for European scripted dramas now, given these latest developments at Netflix, but also following the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros.? The latest Netflix call underlined the growth in terms of viewers of content coming from non-English language countries. We are quite strong in that space. With Italy, of course, Groenlandia being one of the most successful scripted Italian companies. But also in Spain, where we have the company Pokeepsie that just made “Drawn Together” on Amazon that was a fantastic success because they are number one worldwide. We want to continue to invest in that space, flying the European flag with more local stories that can travel globally. Do you think that in macroscopic terms we could be looking at a shift towards a greater amount of high-end TV content productions being shot in the U.S.? Maybe. Yes and no. I think Netflix and the Hollywood studios are all under financial pressure. So they will also look at finding the best balance between finance and creative on high-end things. I think the U.K. is maybe a good bridge between the two. We can produce high-end and premium scripted, as we already do. But we want to continue to grow in that space. We produced “House of Guinness,” which is renewed for season two. We produced “War,” just released on HBO, also a great success. “The Wanted Man” is coming soon on Apple, made with George Kay again. So I think there will be a balance, and that’s also why we really want to invest in the English language market. Bassetti in an impassioned keynote here at MIA underlined the importance of what he called the “European production model.” Can you elaborate on that? We fight a lot for that. Retaining IP is really one of our big fights at the moment, and we are really convinced it’s crucially important for us. And I think the U.K. model works very well, often allowing you to retain 50% of the IP. This allows us to invest in creativity, and our business is based on creativity. Marco said it: ‘we invested one billion euros over the last four years in creativity, because it’s the root of our business. It’s where everything starts. To be able to have the ability to invest in creativity, we need to retain IP. And that’s where the European model sits. title: Alexander Brothers Case Is a “Microcosm for a Lot of Questions about Sexual Assault,” Says Doc Director
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 6:50am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from Peacock’s ‘The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers.’ Courtesy of Peacock Ahead of their sentencing next week in a federal sex-trafficking case, a Peacock documentary is casting a fresh light on the sordid story of the Alexander brothers. The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers , which premieres on Sunday, arrives just as brothers Tal, Oren and Alon Alexander — two of them onetime stars in the flashy world of luxury real estate — face potential life sentences. After being accused of drugging and raping dozens of women in a federal trial earlier this year, they were convicted of sex trafficking, while two of them are still awaiting trial for a state case in Florida. The three-part documentary follows the brothers’ rise from their privileged youth in Miami to reaching the highest echelons of high-end real estate, first at Douglas Elliman and then at their own brokerage, called Official. And it tracks them through their rapid downfall after news broke that two women had filed civil suits against Oren and Alon alleging rape and assault, after which dozens of women came forward with their own grisly accusations. (The brothers have maintained that they never drugged and raped anyone.) The Wolves of Real Estate director Emma Schwartz is no newbie to stories of sexual abuse and violence: She executive produced and co-directed The Fall of Diddy for HBO Max, which tracked accusations surrounding Sean “Diddy” Combs. Still, she says, even with her track record in telling tricky pop-culture investigations with the production company Maxine (she also worked on Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV ), “this one was definitely one of the harder ones” in terms of finding subjects willing to go on camera, she told The Hollywood Reporter . In the interview, Schwartz also discussed a lingering mystery in the brothers’ story, the details of the case that stick with her and the questions that she hopes viewers ask after watching the documentary. The story has been covered pretty intensely in the press. What more did you feel that a documentary could bring to the story? I think a lot of the stories that we like to focus on at Maxine are taking a big look at the story. The day-to-day coverage only tells you part of it. And even the articles that went through a dozen accounts in the summer of 2024, they were sort of part of the buildup of a story. And what you can do with a documentary is you can look at the entirety. How did it begin? What happened before? You can look outside of the walls of a criminal case. You’re right, there were reporters at trial writing articles a number of days, but that only told you part of the story. And part of what we can also do is help raise these bigger questions. Why is it that it takes women so long to come forward? What systems do we have in place to enable women to feel safe coming forward? How much does power and wealth play into the way the justice system goes after cases like this? And so I think there’s a lot of bigger questions that you can see in context in a documentary that you might not understand or see [otherwise]. But beyond that, I think there are really unique accounts that we have from individuals that were not necessarily in the public domain that have not been out there that help you understand people’s relationships with the brothers, the kind of power that they wielded and so much more. Was the process of finding subjects for this project simple or complex? Look, I don’t think anyone who’s done a documentary would ever tell you that it’s an easy thing. Certainly not documentaries that investigate people who are powerful, but I think this one was definitely one of the harder ones. There was a sort of cone of silence around the brothers and people who knew them and a lot of fear still from a lot of the women who, while they had come forward, not a lot of them wanted to actually share that publicly. Even if you look at the trial, a number of women testified under a pseudonym. They wanted to testify, but they didn’t want their name plastered all over the Internet. And I can understand that, right? So this was a really difficult story to get people to speak publicly and it took a lot of fits and starts and there were people that wanted to and then didn’t want to. And that’s part of the process. But I do think in the end, we were able to find people across the eras and in different facets of the brothers’ lives to, at least I hope, tell a fulsome account of both what happened and our best understanding of how some of this may have happened. What surprised you most as you were working on this documentary? There’s always a lot of surprises along the way, and you get to a point where you almost can’t remember what was surprising anymore. But I think one thing I keep coming back to was the way in which the brothers committed so much to writing, so much about the way that they thought about women and the way that they, in their own words, hunted women, preyed on women, and thought of women as something where you could get your return on investment, almost like property. That kind of language is sort of searing. And while we may never understand why people commit sexual assault or exactly what leads to any particular situation, there was clearly this mentality that women were less than, and that they were pretty brazen in how they talked about women, at least among their friends, quite openly. I mean, even messages that never made it in the doc, I still remember. Oh really? There’s this one that was at trial. I mean, I don’t know, it’s all really inappropriate and uncomfortable to say, but there was an exchange with this one woman where she texts Oren and she says, “I woke up with a dick inside of me. That’s not okay.” And he’s like, “Oh, I’m sorry.” And then she’s like, “You have to ask consent before you do that.” And he says, “I used my fingers first.” I mean, I can’t forget that one, and that was part of the evidence at trial. So I think it really was a lot of those messages that stood out. It seems like an interesting challenge as a filmmaker to be in the trial and be able to witness that, but not be able to put it on camera. So how did you look to convey what you saw and witnessed through the film? Yeah, that was an incredible challenge. A lot of documentaries, especially ones in certain states, you have the footage, you have the testimony. We had transcripts, we had court sketches, and then we did obviously have an interview with Lindsey who had testified at trial and journalists who were there. I remember the first cutdown we did of the trial was outrageously long because we’re like, “There were so many things.” But in trying to help people understand what happened at trial, we’re not prosecutors putting on evidence, we’re trying to give you the essence of what happened and not every single detail. And so part of that was laying out the patterns, laying out some of the messages, laying out some of the accounts, laying out videos. The thing about rape and sexual assault is, not always, but more often than not, it’s not like there are witnesses. There’s not someone who saw the bloody knife in a murder, right? And oftentimes they’re very difficult cases because it’s him and it’s her. But in this one instance, there was a woman who didn’t even remember what had happened to her. She had been 17 at the time, and she testified at trial that they seemed to have found her because they found this video on one of the brother’s hard drives. And it was a video in which she was clearly intoxicated, not just with alcohol, but drugs, and Oren engaging in various sex acts and recording it, which resulted in a charge of sexual exploitation of a minor because she was 17 at the time. And so the public never saw that, which thank God, we don’t need to see that, but those 12 jurors had to watch that seven-minute video. And for those seven minutes, it was like a ghost town. It was silent. I think that silence speaks volumes to the intensity of what they were watching. It’s horrible. Were there any parts of the story that you were unable to crack in time to deliver this documentary? One of the things that a lot of people raised was the brothers had friends around them, there were allegations involving the brothers and sometimes a friend, and nobody else was charged with a crime, so what happens to those people is there liability, there’s a lot that remains uncertain about all of those things. But look, with any story, there’s always questions, there’s always things that you wish you could answer and sometimes your job is to lay out the best that you can and raise those questions and hopefully that provokes more from other people. Beyond the specifics of this story, is there any larger message that you hope the series leaves viewers with? Yeah absolutely, and thank you for that question. I think sometimes the timing gods work in your favor here, which is to say that I think we always felt going into this story that as a society, even in the wake of #MeToo, that we had not really reckoned with these questions of what is appropriate behavior? What is predatory? How do we make women feel safe coming forward with sexual assault? And what is the appropriate adjudication and justice for that kind of behavior? We’ve seen really in the last week that these are very live question in our public dialogue and with young people, when you look at all of the conversations around the Jane Doe from Cornell, there are—again, these are different cases — but there are certain themes. Themes about does a woman realize it’s sexual assault right away? In the case of Jane Doe it took her weeks to come to that realization. In the case of some of these women, it took years. The guys at the fraternity said everything that happened, it was consensual. That was at the core of the brothers’ argument — they were playboys, they were not predators. Yes, they had a lot of sex, but that was consensual. And so these are questions that I think we are still reckoning with and that I hope in telling these stories we continue to ask ourselves what should be okay? And try to continue to come to places where more women can feel safe to come forward. I think a big reason people in general participated but especially the women participated was that, I think someone said, “I just hope this never happens again.” They wanted people to learn. And look, we don’t learn from everybody’s experiences perfectly but if somebody can, then I think hopefully we’ve done something. So certainly I think this is a microcosm for a lot of questions about sexual assault, about the way power functions, about the justice system, that we can all learn from, I hope, and go through that journey. Anything else you want to add? The one thing I will just throw out here and this might be a little wonky but I think is really important here is the reason why these women were even able to file these civil lawsuits, it took two women to snowball into these floodgates of dozens of women, but that only happened because there was a special law in New York called the Adult Survivors Act which you no doubt know about, but it had a time window to allow women to come forward with just civil claims that were outside the statue of limitations. That doesn’t exist anymore. And in most states, there are time windows on sexual assault, on when a survivor of sexual assault can come forward and can actually lead to some sort of criminal case. So I think there’s a lot of questions around the system we have today and whether it is designed to, what we know from research is the reality of when people come forward or how people come forward. Which is often not right away and often can take years. So I think there are real questions about whether any of those systems will be reconfigured or repealed. title: Luke Evans on His New ITV Drama ‘The Party,’ Starring in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ on Broadway and Whether He’ll Return as Bard in ‘The Hunt for Gollum’
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:45am PT Luke Evans on His New ITV Drama ‘The Party,’ Starring in ‘The Rocky Horror Picture Show’ on Broadway and Whether He’ll Return as Bard in ‘The Hunt for Gollum’ By K.J. Yossman Plus Icon K.J. Yossman @KJYossman Latest Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ 2 hours ago Prince William Declares His Love for Christopher Nolan Movies and ‘The Traitors’ in Surprise Appearance on ‘The Graham Norton Show’ 4 hours ago Amy Winehouse West End Musical in Development (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source World Productions Luke Evans is among the rare cadre of British actors who regularly balance Hollywood blockbusters with more modest British dramas. Not to mention the actor, who has starred in movies as diverse as “The Hobbit” trilogy and the live-action “Beauty and the Beast” opposite Emma Watson, also recently came off a five-month stint Broadway stint as Frank-N-Furter earlier this year, for which he was nominated for a Tony. His latest project is “The Party,” an adaptation of a psychological thriller by Elizabeth Day, which he also co-produced, for ITV . (The five-part series, which is repped for global sales by ITV Studios, is currently available to watch on ITVX). The show deals with class, hidden sexuality and the nature of both romantic and platonic love all wrapped up in a tense drama. Popular on Variety Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Evans, who first came across Day’s novel as a lockdown read during the Covid pandemic, was instrumental in bringing the series to screen and in getting Sarah Solemani to adapt it (Solemani also plays his wife, Lucy, in the show). Evans sat down with Variety to talk about the differences between the novel and the series, his recent experiences on Broadway and whether Tolkien fans can expect him to reprise his role as Bard the Bowman in Andy Serkis’s upcoming feature “The Hunt for Gollum.” How much did you and Sarah discuss the changes between the source material and the screenplay? When you bring somebody on who has the capability of someone like Sarah, you have to let them run with it, and it was exciting and also daunting to know what she was going to change, but also we knew things would change. The fact that Lucy is pregnant adds another major layer of weight to what is going on in Martin’s head, and also that you know they had a physical relationship, and I think that informs something more about how messed up the life Martin has chosen to live is. There is a love there, and I think that’s another reason why we expanded on their relationship. You see much more of Lucy and Martin together because you want to see that they are a functioning, if slightly unconventional, relationship. I know couples like Martin and Lucy. The other big difference is that Martin in the screen version serves time and he doesn’t in in the novel. What was the thinking behind that change? Putting him into detention to pay the price for someone else, it’s a scar that — he’s tarnished for life. He has a criminal record and lives his life knowing he didn’t do it, I mean it’s huge. It’s massive. What did you want to bring to the character of Martin? Sarah and I had very, very long Zoom calls where she just asked me lots of questions about my upbringing, and of course I started saying I can relate to Martin. I’m a gay man. I’ve come from a very working-class background, and I was presented with opportunities that I took that put me in very alien situations where I didn’t feel comfortable or an insider, but I kept watching, learning, adapting, and trying to fit in. I basically spent my whole life doing that, and that’s who Martin is. I talked about the fact I’m an only child, a very religious background, and Sarah took a lot of those ideas from my life or real things that happened to me and turned them into Martin’s story. So of course, there are slight parallels, which is interesting and it works. Elizabeth revisits the characters in another book, “One of Us.” Does the show lend itself to potentially being returning series? Yeah, absolutely. There is closure for sure within this arc, of course there needs to be, but there are lots of unanswered questions. “One of Us” came out during the end of the shoot, which was exciting and teased us with lots of new ideas. Who knows? As well as “The Party,” there have been a number of shows recently, like Richard Gadd’s “Half Man” and Russell T Davies’ “Tip Toe,” that have explored male relationships and homophobia. Do you think there’s a reason these stories are being told now? As much as we live in a more progressive society, and I think we’re very lucky — I’ve just been in New York and America for seven months, and of course, New York is this little world of its own where everybody can do what the hell they want, and everybody’s accepted — I know that’s not how the country is. I feel that we have progressed in the United Kingdom very far when it comes to equality and it comes to being yourself and an acceptance of each and every one of us. But it’s not by a long shot safe. What we have right now is not safe. You only have to look at the politics, and you have to look at the parties, and some of them, what they’re saying, it’s scary. And I think those kinds of whispers of threat to your life and your existence and your authenticity and your identity can suppress people and can make people hide away, and I do think people do. In my industry I know for a fact that happens. I couldn’t because I was already an openly happy gay man before my movie career began, and so I knew it would become a public knowledge/gossip column idea for a period of my career because I knew people would find out and there was nothing I could do about it and I had to accept it. And then we’re talking about Martin’s industry and the political world, and on top of why Martin suppresses it or hides is because Ben has chosen a certain life, and for Martin to be in Ben’s life, Martin has to be a certain way also. On the other end of the spectrum, you recently played Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” How was that? It was nuts. It was not what I was expecting. In a wonderfully colorful, big way. It delivered on so many levels I wasn’t expecting. I absolutely loved it. Probably one of the hardest things I’ve ever done. After not doing a musical for 18 years, to set foot on a Broadway stage with a Broadway audience in six-[inch] stiletto boots, eight times a week, was a cross-country marathon, I would say, but I loved it, and it was so rewarding. And then to get a Tony nomination, it was — it just kept delivering. Tim Curry, who originated the role and of course played him in the iconic film adaptation, died just after you finished the show. Had you spoken to him about it? I wrote a letter to him two weeks before I finished the show, and I sent it to him, and his team gave it to him, and he said he was very appreciative of the letter, and then two weeks later I finished the show, and a day after that he died. I was part of that final show that was associated with him and him with us. And he was in my mind every day. I had a picture of him in my dressing room, and so I’m just so grateful I sent the letter and that I was part of that incredible show. It was magical. Another cult project you’ve been involved with of course is Peter Jackson’s Tolkien adaptations, having starred as Bard the Bowman in “The Hobbit” trilogy. Are you returning for Andy Serkis’ sequel, “The Hunt for Gollum”? Well, if I’m correct, Bard is a human. I don’t think he would have been born, or is he dead? Is it in between? It’s in between. But how far after “The Hobbit” is it? I think there’s approximately 60 years between “The Hobbit” and “The Lord of the Rings” and “The Hunt for Gollum” will be set in between – so Bard could come back. Yeah, I think Bain, my son, could be in it. But I think Bard doesn’t. Take me back to Wellington. I’d love to go! title: Why Judd Apatow Puts Himself in (Most of) His Documentaries
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 23, 2026 6:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Judd Apatow and Maria Bamford in 'Paralyzed by Hope: The Maria Bamford Story.' Netflix Right now, Netflix’s stock price (NFLX) is a joke — just not the funny, ha-ha kind. Simultaneously, the Netflix Is a Joke branding is bringing subscribers four documentaries on four comedy entities — Martin Mull (Oct. 7), Norm Macdonald (Oct. 16), Maria Bamford (Oct. 23) and SCTV (Oct. 30) — this month. Judd Apatow, a comedy legend in his own right, directed two of them: he made Norm’s solo and Maria’s with Neil Berkeley, who also co-directed Martin’s (with Bob Saget; Jason Hehir directed the SCTV documentary). (To proactively clear any confusing, the Netflix Is a Joke festival is not happening this month. Robbie Praw, Netflix’s vice president of standup and comedy formats told THR that Netflix Is a Joke is “more than a festival — it’s an ecosystem and lens for how we think about stand-up comedy,” adding, “These documentaries are part of that and take it further: Honoring four comedy icons… and keeping the conversation going all year round.”) The individual films are as different as the individuals they chronicle. Apatow ( Knocked Up , The 40-Year-Old Virgin ) often inserts himself as an on-screen supporting character in his documentaries — like his prior Mel Brooks and Garry Shandling films — as he does again with Paralyzed By Hope: The Maria Bamford Story . The first voice we hear after the Paralyzed by Hope title screen is Apatow’s. The first face we see in its present-day footage is Apatow’s. It’s not a vanity thing. Apatow believes the camera following him is “a way to make [the film] more personal,” and in cases like the Shandling doc, to show “what it was like to be his friend and mentee,” he told The Hollywood Reporter . It’s a user-experience thing: as a viewer, Apatow likes to know to whom a documentary’s subjects are talking at any given time. “Those conversations are very intimate, and the obsession with eliminating the idea that someone asks a question sometimes takes away a level that reveals something about the subject,” Apatow said. “If I’m talking to Mel Brooks, he’s talking in a specific way because it’s me … It’s being honest with the audience that this isn’t exactly normal.” Neil Berkeley ( Gilbert , Harmontown ) is not famous, which can also work to one’s advantage. When making his Gilbert Gottfried doc, Berkeley just moved in with the comedian (a la Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything — except, you know, nothing at all like what goes down in You Can See Everything ). “I’m not in my movies. I’ve always been very against that. Not for any other reason other than, who wants to see me in this movie?” Berkeley said. His Paralyzed By Hope colleague is “a known commodity,” Berkeley added, so Apatow being on screen “makes sense.” The differing approaches, which converged somewhat in Paralyzed By Hope , are equally legit, Netflix’s vp of original documentaries Adam Del Deo, told THR . It is what we don’t see that makes for the best biographical documentaries, he said. “What we(‘ve) found is this,” Del Deo explained. “To create this authenticity, it’s about filmmakers building trust and getting intimacy with the subjects. In doing that, there’s ability to dig deeper into their lives, what makes them tick, and it creates this relatability.” ‘Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald.’ Netflix Apatow made Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald the Berkeley way. “The approach there was to do a found-footage documentary about Norm because he’s such an unreliable narrator. You don’t really know when he’s telling the truth or trying to be provocative or just making things up for fun in a very Bob Dylan-esque way,” Apatow said. “So, we made the decision to just arrange moments from his life and career, and let the audience decide what it all adds up to.” Also: Norm died in 2021, so it necessitated a different format. The “brilliance” of the Macdonald doc , Berkeley said, stems from his theory that “the best documentaries feel like their subjects … that movie feels like everyone these days’ experience with Norm Macdonald.” If you don’t get that, just search Norm’s name on YouTube. You can easily spend hours spiraling down through a rabbit hole of material and stories, laughing the whole time. And when you finally come up for air, you still won’t know who was the real Norm Macdonald and what was one big joke on all of us. No one will fault Apatow for switching his styles up — probably. When it’s your money financing the film, as Apatow says he did “for years” for the Bamford doc, pretty much anything goes. Paralyzed By Hope features two different scenes in which Apatow forks over some of that sweet, sweet Girls money to Bamford. At their on-screen meet cute, Apatow hands Bamford $500 cash just to pitch her on her own documentary. The scene was real, Apatow said. “She did say to me, ‘Bring $500.’ I knew she wasn’t kidding,” Apatow said. “She’s very into talking about money. She’s very transparent… She’s been in Debtors Anonymous for decades even though she never went bankrupt.” And she won’t for at least a few more years: the film effectively ends with Apatow handing Bamford a satchel full of cash. He’d eventually be reimbursed by Netflix. Knowing Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos’ strong affinity for Bamford’s comedy, Apatow figured that would happen. “We thought somehow this is going to land at Netflix. I don’t know how, but,” Apatow said. “The whole roll of the dice was at the end of the day, will Ted [Sarandos] like this enough? And we showed it to him, and he loved it the way only a mega, mega Maria fan would love it.” Who Is Martin Mull? wouldn’t have happened without Sarandos either. “The only reason that got finished is we got through a sizzle [reel] and a deck, and Martin had died, and they sent it to Ted, and Ted called the producers and was like, ‘Why didn’t anyone tell me about this? Why didn’t Bob [Saget] tell me about this?’ And he was kind of upset. He said, ‘In case you didn’t know, my first date in high school was a Martin Mull concert,'” Berkeley told THR . “So really, Ted was like the reason that movie is in the world at all.” (Sarandos appears in both docs, and fun fact, owns a dozen Martin Mull paintings.) Del Deo might take slight exception to that innocent statement. “I’ve learned a lot from [Ted] around comedy,” Del Deo said of his final boss Sarandos. “He’s a student of it. But when it comes to programming, those decisions are left up to the documentary team, and these were just great stories.” Three of the four great stories are available now on Netflix; the SCTV documentary premieres one week from today. title: Meghan Markle Says She’s Kept Her Children From Her Father “to Protect Them” In Wake of Child Abuse Image Allegations

Courtesy of Getty Meghan Markle is “deeply distressed” by the news that her father, Thomas Markle, is being investigated for possessing child sex abuse images, and has revealed she’s kept her children from him “for one reason: to protect them.” In a report by Rupert Murdoch-owned tabloid The Sun on Thursday, the Duchess of Sussex’s father, now 82, is said to have been reported to authorities by his own son, Thomas Markle Jr., who told police there were “hundreds, if not thousands” of illegal images in Markle’s Philippines home, the British outlet said. I could never do what I’m being accused of. title: ‘Clueless’ Inspired Kim Kardashian to Buy This Priceless Monet
full_text: × Skip to main content Storm Off the Coasts of Belle-Ile, by Claude Monet, 1886. Oil on canvas. Says Kardashian of another Monet she purchased: This is “the first real piece of art that I bought — myself. Because in Clueless, they called the girls ‘a Monet’ if they look good from afar, but up close they’re just a mess.” Leemage/Corbis Via Getty Images/ One day in early February 2022, I was hanging out at Kim’s office as she tried to cram two cover shoots into one day. Between the shoots, Kim was back in her glam room, getting RE-glammed with different hair and new makeup, this time to shoot the cover of Vogue Hong Kong. Kim was effusive and bossy, running her multibillion-dollar business in a bathrobe, two gay men pulling at her hair and face. At one point, as she was helped into and then out of a complicated, totally sheer Schiaparelli tulle dress — it was pretty much nothing but scaffolding — I looked up from my phone and she was entirely naked. Neither of us flinched. Lately, she and I had been playing a little game of “Guess What Happened in 1995?” because we kept being surprised by the astonishing number of cultural and technological shifts — to say nothing of her own complicated personal circumstances — that unfolded in that one year. Once she was dressed and sitting back in her chair, I said to Kim, “You know what else happened in 1995?” She looked at me expectantly. The movie Clueless came out (her favorite film). When it was first released, Kim and her father (and a group of Kim’s friends and their fathers) all went to see it together. “We were dying at every reference,” she told me. “It was so me in high school. … I had pretty much every outfit that the girls wore in Clueless . … I was still into Contempo Casuals and shopping at Judy’s at the Century City Mall. … Like, when I saw that movie, I couldn’t believe it. Clueless is still, to this day, my favorite movie. It really resonated.” Related Stories Lifestyle Kim Kardashian Read Every Page of Her Authorized Biography. Here's What She Pushed Back On. Beyond the Book "Respect Rather Than Reverence": Inside the Making of a Grittier 'Sense and Sensibility' Clueless , inspired by Jane Austen’s Emma , stars Alicia Silverstone as Cher Horowitz, a ditzy but well-meaning rich girl living in the ultraprivileged bubble of her Beverly Hills high school. “I just wanted this fake world that you would see in a comedy of manners about the turn of the century,” director Amy Heckerling said in an interview, adding, “Positivity fascinates me — I don’t understand it … so I started to think about a character that would be so happy and sure things would work out.” A character like Kim. Clueless was written and directed in 1994, right as Kim was entering her freshman year at Marymount High School, and right as her family was becoming a fixture in the inescapable O.J. Simpson news cycle. Heckerling’s highly tuned antennae capture such a specific moment of Beverly Hills youth culture; it’s hard to believe something of Kim’s life wasn’t absorbed from the ether. Cher goes to the mall and shops at Contempo Casuals and Fred Segal. She is obsessed with her closet, the organization of which puts even Kim to shame. Cher’s iconic yellow plaid outfit evoked Kim’s Catholic school girl uniform as imagined by Donatella Versace. Kim and Kourtney and their friends carpooled to school, blasting hip-hop in a white BMW, while Cher drives her friends in a white Jeep Wrangler. Cher famously volunteers to be “captain of the Pismo Beach disaster relief” effort, while Kim spent Coastal Cleanup Day scouring the Santa Monica beaches for trash. All of the scenes in the ostentatiously enormous house where Cher lives with her strict, attorney father (who happens to look exactly like O.J. lawyer Robert Shapiro) were shot in a 10,000-square-foot house in Encino, just down the road from Robert Kardashian’s 11,000-square-foot former home on Mandalay Drive, which, much like the fictional Horowitz residence, features a grand double staircase. As their homes become the prep site for a big trial, Kim and Cher both take an interest in their father’s legal work. Ripped straight from the headlines, Cher calls her brother-in-law Josh a “Kato” — as in Kato Kaelin, one of the minor witnesses in the O.J. trial — meaning “freeloader.” Amy Heckerling’s 1995 hit Clueless , starring Stacey Dash (left) and Alicia Silverstone, is Kardashian’s favorite film: “It was so me in high school. … I had pretty much every outfit that the girls wore in it. I was still into Contempo Casuals and shopping at Judy’s at the Century City Mall.” ©Paramount/Courtesy Everett Collection Much of the infamous slang from the film — the texture that provides the crackling authenticity — came from Heckerling’s impeccable ear for the way people really talk (gay men, stoners, rappers), but there was another source, one with surprising proximity to Kim. “I have to give props to the UCLA linguistics department,” said Heckerling. “They published a list of slang words and phrases, and Monet came from that.” (As Cher explains to Dionne: “She’s a full-on Monet. It’s like a painting, see? From far away it’s OK, but up close it’s a big ol’ mess.”) You could literally throw a rock from Kim’s high school parking lot at Marymount across Sunset and it would land on the UCLA campus. Seniors at Marymount often walked over to hang out in the quad. All of which is to say, some of the ’90s slang collected by the students at UCLA may very well have been uttered by Marymount students. In Kim’s glam room, as she was explaining why Clueless is her favorite movie — indeed, the impact it had on her teenage years — she said, “And that’s the reason I bought my Monet.” I stared at her and blinked a couple of times. “The first real piece of art that I bought — myself — was a Monet. Because in the movie they called the girls ‘a Monet’ if they look good from afar, but up close they’re just a mess.” I was still staring and blinking, trying not to let on how extravagantly implausible this sounded. Kim bought a Monet not because she had visited the famous Water Lilies at l’Orangerie in Paris or under the art world tutelage of Kanye West. She bought a Monet for the same reason she kept the box of chicken McNuggets from her first date with TJ Jackson — a piece of high school nostalgia. A sketch of Kardashian’s Tadao Ando-designed concrete house in Palm Springs on her Instagram. @kimkardashian/Instagram She continued: “I was in Italy, and it was being auctioned, and I was with Kim Jones [creative director of Fendi], and we were doing our Fendi/Skims fitting in Rome. I really wanted this Monet painting because it’s a gray Monet — a pretty landscape, but gray. … I really wanted it for my Tadao Ando house in Palm Springs, which is all concrete. And I’m bidding and I’m bidding, and it was the first auction that I ever did, so I didn’t really know how they worked. But you get really into it. So Kim Jones is there with me and he’s like, “GET IT!” So I bid on it. I win. And I went over what my budget was because you’re in the moment.” And then, in true Cher Horowitz fashion, a blunder straight out of a comedy of manners: “So, I got it. It’s delivered. And it’s like … THIS big. Like, a postcard. I didn’t think to check the dimensions! I thought it was going to cover a whole wall! I’m going to put it in my Ando when it’s done,” she says, laughing. “Like in the powder room.” Excerpted from Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter. Copyright 2026. title: Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:30am PT Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest Despite Hudson Williams, Canadian Witch Mystery ‘Yaga’ Is No ‘Heated Rivalry’: TV Review 32 minutes ago ‘The Gilded Age’ Team on Paramount Merger Parallels and Going From Budget Cuts to a Season 3 Breakout: ‘You’re Part of a Very Fortunate Minority’ 23 hours ago Olivia Cooke on Returning to ‘Slow Horses,’ On-Set Injuries and That Shocking Finale Cliffhanger: ‘I Want a Showdown!’ 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of AMC+ The witchy thriller “ Yaga ” is a Canadian production that co-stars Hudson Williams, now hot enough off of “Heated Rivalry” to earn a “with” before his name in the credits. That’s about where the similarities with the hockey-themed megahit end, though not for lack of trying: “Yaga” — which airs on streaming service AMC+ in the States — painfully strains for the eroticism and insight into sexuality that came so easily to “Heated Rivalry,” resulting in an eight-episode season that’s often cringe without ascending into camp. But other blunders are all “Yaga”’s own. Choppy pacing, poor casting and facile feminism all combine to make “Yaga” a misfire, one viewers in search of seasonal scares should overlook in favor of alternatives. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ Adapted by creator Kat Sandler from her play of the same name, “Yaga” introduces itself as a missing persons mystery centered on Williams’ Henry Park, a billionaire heir whose concerned parents send family fixer Rapp (Noah Reid) to track down somewhere in rural British Columbia. But the story’s real interest is right there in the title: Sandler wants to rework the Baba Yaga myth of cannibal witches in chicken-legged huts for the modern day. (“Yaga” foreshadows this project with Slavic covers of various pop standards, a legitimately fun detail.) Unfortunately, the show can’t muster a take more interesting than platitudes like “a witch is just someone society has decided they’re afraid of,” coming more than a decade after touchstones like “The Witch” and “American Horror Story: Coven” advanced similar ideas in a more artful way. Popular on Variety “Yaga” could deliver excitement in other areas, and tries to. Rapp quickly discovers Henry and his lookalike roommate Logan (also Williams, minus colored contacts and plus a prosthetic nose), both college students, had an uncommonly close relationship with their professor Katherine (Carrie-Ann Moss), an anthropologist known as the “bone lady” for her academic interest in ossified remains. When he meets Katherine in a hotel bar, not realizing she’s about to be a person of interest, Rapp’s idea of a come-on is asking for sexy facts about bones. Such clumsy and futile attempts at chemistry are not the fault of Moss, who’s pretty much the only person in the ensemble to project the earthy, seductive vibe “Yaga” is clearly going for. Rapp himself is part of the problem: Reid’s performance renders him a loudmouth bro whose effect on the town’s women, including but by no means limited to Katherine, utterly baffling. (At times, the question of Rapp’s inexplicable attractiveness is more pressing than that of Henry’s whereabouts.) There’s also a clash between the gorgeous, haunting atmosphere implied by the scenery, all fog-bound waters and shady forests, and the buddy-cop banter between Rapp and his quasi-partner Carson (Clark Backo), a local police officer he mocks for being mannish — or even, gasp, gay! “Yaga” can’t manage the ramp-up from such crass comments to the eerie and metaphysical, with the elements forming a discordant clash rather than a smooth blend. If there’s an archetype more overdone than the witch who’s actually a misunderstood outcast, it’s the rich guy who’s secretly into sinister sex stuff. Sure enough, the ghost of Jeffrey Epstein begins to haunt “Yaga” as Rapp and Carson start to uncover what Henry and Logan have been up to — namely, house parties suffused with bisexual lighting and the occasional chicken sacrifice. Rather than alluring or even disgusting, the details of Henry and Logan’s trysts are almost juvenile in their attempts to provoke; the particulars of who’s sleeping with who, and under what circumstances, are filled with over-the-top and unconvincing details, jumping the shark from the salacious to the outright criminal in the blink of an eye. By the time “Yaga” arrives at its inevitable reversals of perpetrator and victim, whatever spell (get it?) the show’s cast on the audience has long since been broken. Already offputting, Reid’s performance of Rapp’s dawning realizations — flipping from dismissive skepticism to feverish belief with little in between — grows less grounded by the minute. To be fair, the fault here lies equally with the scripts, which dump information without first creating suspense. Perhaps there’s a reason most horror dramas don’t have quick, 30-minute episodes, though the prospect of an even longer “Yaga” is not an enticing one. The first two episodes of “Yaga” are now streaming on AMC+, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Fridays.
