title: You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:30am PT You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest You Can See Everything, Except Outside North America: Inside A24’s Staggered International Release Strategy for Nathan Fielder’s Hit Elizabeth Holmes Doc 31 minutes ago Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones Support ‘Normal People’ Author Sally Rooney After U.K. Book Ban: She’s a ‘Writer, Not a Terrorist’ 2 days ago The Beatles Immersive Experience, Featuring Sets and Props From Sam Mendes’ Biopics, Set for Liverpool 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of A24 A24 ’s “ You Can See Everything ” has become one of the year’s biggest box office surprises, opening to a staggering $15.6 million in the U.S. and generating a frenzy of headlines, spoilers, memes and online chatter. But for audiences outside North America, catching Nathan Fielder’s three-hour documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes — now expected to be a major player in awards season — has become a frustrating waiting game. Despite the film’s blockbuster debut — the second-biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary, behind “Fahrenheit 9/11” — A24 isn’t releasing it in the U.K. and Australia until Nov. 20, more than a month after its U.S. bow. Sony Pictures, which recently acquired the film for several international territories, including Germany, Latin America and South Korea, has yet to announce its release plans. Related Stories Lara Croft’s Inaugural Voice Actor Shelley Blond Recalls First Time She Saw ‘Tomb Raider’ Character: ‘I Thought She Was Very Sexy and Very Ballsy’ As one producer jokingly put it in a message to Variety : “You Can See Everything, unless you live outside N. America.” Popular on Variety The frustration was palpable at the BFI London Film Festival, where excited speculation was mounting that the documentary would be unveiled as the surprise screening on Oct. 16. With co-director Lance Oppenheim in town earlier that week (for his other film, “Primetime”) and a special BAFTA screening having taken place that afternoon, many festivalgoers were convinced “You Can See Everything” was heading to the Royal Festival Hall. Instead, the surprise screening turned out to be Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky.” The delay raises a broader question about A24’s international release strategy at a time when social media can turn a film into a global cultural event overnight. Because “You Can See Everything” isn’t alone among the studio’s titles that make non-U.S. audiences sit tight, something that has been widely lamented online. Oppenheim’s Robert Pattinson starring “Primetime” released in the U.S. on Sep. 25, becoming A24’s third biggest opening with $19.2 million after “Backrooms” and “Civil War.” U.K. previews kick off on Oct. 28, just days before it gets VOD launch in the U.S. (like “You Can See Everything,” Sony picked up the film for numerous other territories). Back in 2022, A24’s megahit and Oscar winner “Everything Everywhere All at Once” released in the U.K. a full two months after bowing in the U.S. And then there’s another of 2026’s most hotly-anticipated titles, “Club Kid,” which is suffering a similar fate. Jordan Firstman’s acclaimed directorial debut and Cannes breakout lands in cinemas in the U.S on Nov. 6. In the U.K.? Jan. 8, 2027. There are, of course, several factors at play. A24 — which wouldn’t comment on its release strategy for this article — only self-distributes outside North America in a couple of territories, notably the U.K./Ireland and Australia/New Zealand, and even then many of its titles go through a third party (the films named above were all handled solely by A24). There’s also the long-held sense that having an advanced U.S. campaign is extremely beneficial to help test the waters and serve as a momentum-building ice-breaker for the overseas trip. “But for a film that is so spoiler-heavy as ‘You Can See Everything,’ a month is extraordinary,” notes one Brit doc publicity veteran. It should be noted that last Christmas’ extremely buzzy A24 release “Marty Supreme” came out in the U.K. less than a week after the U.S. and grossed in excess of $22 million, the studio’s biggest success on British shores to date. But perhaps “You Can See Everything” is a very unique case. After all, very few people outside of the inner A24-Fielder-Oppenheim circle knew anything about it before its shock Telluride screening. As one insider notes, “The film really didn’t exist in the world until six weeks ago.” A24 has had a tight turnaround to get it into U.S. cinemas since then. Perhaps a simultaneous or near-simultaneous launch in the U.K. — where it has an office overseeing local productions but no dedicated distribution team — was a step too far (especially given it’s gearing up to release “Primetime” as well). There’s also the possibility that simply few expected “You Can See Everything” — a documentary almost as long as “Oppenheimer” and about a disgraced and overexposed Silicon Valley founder who has already been the center of a hit TV drama — to become such a theatrical juggernaut. Was the power of Fielder and this stunt release underestimated? Not so — at least not among those who know documentaries — claims the publicity vet. “Within the very rarefied documentary world, the minute it was announced, everyone knew it was going be huge,” they say. “Maybe A24 isn’t plugged in as much, but as soon as Elizabeth Holmes’ face popped up, everyone was just like, ‘Well that’s just blown ‘NAZA’ out.'” In terms of timing, to launch in the U.K. on the same date as the U.S. would have seen “You Can See Everything” go up against fellow new releases in the video game adaptation “Streetfighter” and animated feature “Forgotten Island” (and not, unlike America, the closest potential rival in terms of audiences, “Sense & Sensibility”). That said, the U.K. is about to go into school half-term holidays, not generally suited, at least when it comes to more mainstream-focused cinemas, for arthouse-focused indies. “If someone had tried to get us to put a 3-hour doc in our cinemas just ahead of half term, we probably wouldn’t have even answered their calls,” says one exhibition exec, who admits his audiences tend to lean much more towards the popcorn titles. “This is just the wrong type and shape of film for us during that period, which is more horror classics and family fun.” The exec suggests that a post-holiday early November release might have been more strategic, but then that would put “You Can See Everything” firmly on the heels of “Primetime.” A month-long delay to see a film the entire internet appears to be talking about might be excruciatingly frustrating — especially for those desperately now trying to avoid the spoiler-filled articles and posts littering social media. But the wait and anticipation do appear to have done wonders for pre-sales. According to a report in The Guardian earlier this week, tickets at London’s Picturehouse Central cinema went on sale before its U.S. opening, with the demand forcing the chain to put on additional screenings. It was a similar situation at Cineworld, which has added more screenings at its major Leicester Square site and expanded bookings elsewhere after the initial batch of tickets sold out. Variety has since heard that Australia’s Palace Cinemas — which operates in 25 locations across the country — has just broken the record for single-day pre-sales with “You Can See Everything.” Such was the demand for tickets for Fielder’s wild, genre-flipping documentary that sales doubled that of the previous record holder: “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.” ‘Billions’ and ‘John Wick 3’ Star Asia Kate Dillon Says Acting Jobs Have ‘Diminished’ and They’re in Need of Customer Service Work Loading comments...

title: Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Jonathan Groff Returning To Broadway In Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’ ‘The Imaginary Invalid’ Broadway Review: Molière Gets Clowned By A Winning Bill Irwin Neil DeGrasse Tyson, Bill Nye & Mae Jemison Join Broadway’s ‘Galileo’ Musical As Co-Producers View All October 23, 2026 6:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jonathan Groff, Jessica Dickey, Sarna Lapine Chad Meyer/Production Tony Award winner Jonathan Groff will return to Broadway this winter in The Amish Project , a solo play written by Jessica Dickey and directed by Sarna Lapine. Performances begin Wednesday, February 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre. Producers Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy announced the show and its star today. An official opening night is yet to be announced, and the design team will be announced shortly. Coming off two very successful big-cast Broadway projects – Merrily We Roll Along and Just In Time – Groff will now go solo in The Amish Project , a play described by the production as “a deeply moving solo play about the astonishing power of compassion in the face of unimaginable loss.” Related Stories News 'The Imaginary Invalid' Broadway Review: Molière Gets Clowned By A Winning Bill Irwin News Neil DeGrasse Tyson, Bill Nye & Mae Jemison Join Broadway's 'Galileo' Musical As Co-Producers The synopsis: “When tragedy shatters a close-knit Amish community, what follows is an extraordinary act of grace that challenges everything we think we know about forgiveness. Inspired by true events that unfolded just minutes from where Groff grew up, The Amish Project is an intimate portrait of a place and a community channeled through a single performer. Written by acclaimed playwright Jessica Dickey ( The Rembrandt, The Convent) and directed by Sarna Lapine ( Call Me Izzy, Sunday in the Park with George ), this remarkable story invites us to reflect on how, even in the darkest of hours, our shared humanity endures.” Watch on Deadline Said Groff, “Twenty years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team.” The Amish Project debuted to critical acclaim at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since become Dickey’s most-produced play, with productions at the Guthrie Theater (Minneapolis), Milwaukee Rep, American Theater Company (Chicago) and City Theatre (Pittsburgh), among others at theaters around the world. Producers Ahrens and Kirdahy said in a statement, “We are honored to bring Jessica Dickey’s stirring and luminous play to Broadway, under the direction of the visionary Sarna Lapine. There is nothing quite like experiencing the singular Jonathan Groff live, and his humanity, generosity and gift for storytelling make this a deeply transporting night of theater that we are proud to share with audiences.” Playwright Dickey said, “I wrote The Amish Project in the heartbreak of my twenties, grappling with how to make a meaningful life as an artist in a world capable of such violence. The play launched my writing career and changed my life. To return to it now, all these years later, when its questions feel as urgent as ever, is profoundly moving. And to do so alongside Jonathan Groff, whose personal connection to this story is matched by his staggering talent, and the extraordinary Sarna Lapine, with the steadfast belief and care of Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, is a gift I could never have imagined. I can’t wait for Broadway audiences to see it—I’ll be the playwright in the back laughing and crying.” Director Lapine said, “When I first read Jessie’s play, I was blown away by it. She has channeled something extraordinary about a community, a community in mourning, a community in conversation. It is a piece that stays with you for days, weeks, months, years after you’ve sat with it. Like the framework of a well-built one-room schoolhouse, the writing is precise, lean, and strong, illuminating resilience in the face of fragility, and asks, how does one forgive the unforgivable?” ‘Top Gun’, ‘Picket Fences’ And ‘Alien’ Star Dies At 93; Career In Photos ‘Clayface’ Solid $3.5M Thursday Previews; Can He Scare Off Elizabeth Holmes? title: Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review
full_text: Oct 23, 2026 6:15am PT Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review By Aramide Tinubu Plus Icon Aramide Tinubu Latest Jamie Lee Curtis, Téa Leoni and Tim Daly Lead NBC’s Refreshing and Witty Sitcom ‘Newlyweds’: TV Review 36 minutes ago ‘Other Desert Cities’ Broadway Review: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Ed Harris and Allison Janney Lead a Resounding Family Drama 4 days ago Netflix’s ‘Victorious’ Spinoff ‘Hollywood Arts’ Is a Bland Copy of Shows From a Past Era: TV Review 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Nicole Weingart/NBC Sitcoms aren’t what they used to be. Though a select few on network television, like “Abbott Elementary” and “Ghosts,” pay homage to comedies of the past while tapping into present-day culture, sitcoms today rarely feel truly universal. NBC ’s “ Newlyweds ,” co-created by Jamie Lee Curtis and (the since-fired) Gail Lerner, is fun and refreshing, speaking to a collective audience across generations. Set in present-day Los Angeles, “Newlyweds” begins with a blind date. James ( Tim Daly ), a reserved college professor, sits anxiously in a restaurant, awaiting Jeanie ( Téa Leoni ), a free-spirited middle school teacher who is trying to decide whether she even wants to meet James. After individually deciding to bail on the dinner, the pair run into each other by the valet, and their mutual attraction, despite their vastly different personalities, leads to a spicy evening together. The duo initially believes that they are just having a fling, especially when James’ work sends him to Norway for a month. However, the couple’s connection continues to blossom, and they end up marrying in Las Vegas just six weeks after meeting. Despite their whirlwind romance, neither James nor Jeanie anticipates how different their lives are. Jeanie is enmeshed with her adult children, Poppy (Emma Meisel) and Lolo (Ignacio Diaz-Silverio), who still live at home. Meanwhile, James’ meddling ex-wife, Claudia (Jamie Lee Curtis), remains an aggravating fixture in his otherwise buttoned-up existence. Across the 13-episode first season (critics received three episodes for review), the pair immerse themselves in a newlywed bubble while trying to embrace the chaotic family and friends who orbit them — often infiltrating their private moments. Real-life couple Leoni and Daly work wonderfully as a later-in-life couple, invigorated by this new romantic chapter as they navigate long-held histories, patterns and preferences. Though the duo forms a gentle, tenderhearted center, the ensemble as a whole elevates “Newlyweds,” allowing it to stand above so many recent middling entries in the sitcom space. While all of the episodes provided have their amusing moments, Episode 3, “We’ll Never Have Paris,” is the best of the bunch. During the episode, Jeanie and James’ mini-moon plans are constantly interrupted by Claudia and Jeanie’s children. James even tries to comfort a distraught Poppy after a breakup. Still, the banter between Claudia and Arvid (Bill O’Neill), aka Milky, James’ Norwegian-born teaching assistant, consistently stands out throughout the show. As Claudia, Curtis is perfectly biting and obnoxious, willing to insert herself into her ex-husband’s life for sport, stomping on his feeble boundaries. However, it’s O’Neill’s turn as Arvid that elevates the series. Like Sean Hayes’ Jack McFarland in “Will & Grace,” O’Neill has perfect comedic timing, throwing himself into every aspect of the character’s physical comedy with energetic vibrancy. What’s more, because the couple moves between two worlds — Jeanie’s modest city bungalow with all its warmth and Gen Z angst, and James’ museum-like suburban estate — viewers see how differently the pair live, and the shenanigans they get into when forced outside their respective comfort zones. These days, it’s rare to actually laugh out loud to sitcoms, which is why “Newlyweds” is already off to a stellar start. The cast works like a well-oiled machine, and the characters feel tangible, as if the audience lives next door. Interestingly, Lerner, who co-created the series with Curtis and served as showrunner for the first six episodes, was recently fired because of “creative differences,” and “The Conners” co-creator Bruce Helford has been brought in to replace her for the duration of the season. Whether the show builds on its already solid foundation or collapses in on itself will be fascinating to watch. For now, “Newlyweds” feels refreshing and enjoyable. title: Kim Kardashian Read Every Page of Her Authorized Biography. Here’s What She Pushed Back On.
full_text: × Skip to main content Illustrated By Christopher Hughes Jonathan Van Meter, the legendary magazine writer and editor, has spent much of his career getting unusually close to famous women. His intimate profiles on cultural powerhouses like Oprah Winfrey, Jennifer Aniston, Jodie Foster, Liza Minnelli and Lady Gaga, to name a few, have appeared in the pages of Esquire , Vanity Fair , New York and Vogue , among scores of other glossies. I have known Jonathan for more than 30 years, since we were both came of age in New York magazine publishing during its last golden age, the early 1990s. He is a gifted reporter, a superb raconteur and, as anyone who knows him will attest, a man with very strong feelings about practically everything. Related Stories Beyond the Book "Respect Rather Than Reverence": Inside the Making of a Grittier 'Sense and Sensibility' TV 'Fourth Wing' Author Breaks Silence on Casting, Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya to Star as Violet and Xaden So when he told me during the pandemic that he intended to devote the next several years to writing a biography of Kim Kardashian , I was intrigued — and skeptical. Kardashian might be the most extensively documented woman of her generation. Between reality television, social media and a bottomless tabloid appetite, what could possibly remain to discover? And how would a writer who specializes in emotional complexity get beneath the exquisitely managed surface of someone who has built a billion-dollar-scale public identity around revealing herself while simultaneously giving almost nothing away? The result is Citizen Kim , an authorized biography that took five years to report and write. Van Meter spent time in Kardashian’s homes, accompanied her to photo shoots, watched her conduct business and interviewed dozens of people from across her life. He also discovered that access has its own complications. Kardashian read the manuscript, objected to some passages and, according to Van Meter, ultimately accepted almost all of them. He, meanwhile, found himself increasingly protective of his subject — a predicament he discussed with his therapist. I am aware that one old friend interviewing another about the hazards of getting too close to your subject carries its own set of ironies. We talked anyway, about the handshake deal that got him in the door, Kim’s infamous sex tape, the people he didn’t get to talk to him (Kanye West, Ray J and Paris Hilton, who canceled 17 times) and whether a biographer can fall in love with his subject and still find a way to tell the truth about her. You’re in the thick of your press tour right now. How’s it going? I did three interviews this morning: Dutch, German, German. For some reason, the fucking Germans love this book. But there’s no book tour, no in-person events, no book party. It’s all Zoom and podcasts. I put on some lip balm, throw on a nice shirt and sit down in my office. What’s interesting is seeing what people take. The Daily Mail paid the U.K. publisher a lot of money for an excerpt and cherry-picked everything remotely scandalous. It was the opposite of the book I was trying to write. But the publisher had the right to do it. Are there still people who simply refuse to take her seriously? Every day. Some people hear you’re writing about Kim Kardashian, and their face sinks. When Vanity Fair ran an excerpt and collaborated with me on Instagram, a ton of comments came into my feed. I’d never really studied them. There’s a group that says, “She’s only famous because of a sex tape. It’s not that deep, bro.” They don’t want analysis of any kind. When Kim finally followed me on Instagram, people started sending messages asking me to get their clothing lines to her. She hadn’t even followed me during the five years I was writing the book. Clockwise: Magazine writer and editor Jonathan Van Meter. Lady Gaga spotted leaving Chez André in 2010 in Paris (Van Meter is second from left). From left: Van Meter, Renée Zellweger and artist Ross Bleckner in 2005. Kendall Jenner ran out of gas in Beverly Hills in 2016, the year that Van Meter wrote about Kendall for her first Vogue cover and in the process met Kris Jenner and Kim Kardashian. Jason Schmidt/Marc Piasecki/Filmmagic/Fameflynet.uk.com/Splashnews.com/Lisa Mauceri/Filmmagic Why Kim? You could have chosen any number of subjects. I wrote a Vogue cover story about her in 2019. When it came out, she called me from Bali, at three in the morning, and said, “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you.” I said, “I’m going to write a book about you someday.” Then the pandemic happened, I drank for three months, I sobered up, and I thought, “What am I going to do? Why not a book about Kim?” I talked to my agent, Todd Shuster, and began texting her. There was never any resistance. I could tell she was game. Eventually I said I was coming to L.A. for three months in the summer of 2021. And I started going to her house. Nothing was ever signed. She stayed committed for five years. I thought it would take two years, and so did she, but she never bailed. That seems extraordinary for somebody so famously controlling of her image. What were the ground rules? My agent talked to her lawyer. We called it the Todd Summit because they were both named Todd. The only precondition was that Kim got to read the book for fact-checking. Nobody said, “You can’t talk to these people,” or, “She won’t discuss that.” We just jumped in. It made me wonder whether the idea that she’s controlling about everything is wrong. Maybe this is how she is. But “fact-checking” can mean different things to different people. What happened when she disliked something? She did her homework. She went through it page by page: “Page 33, this is wrong. That was 2002.” Then we had a Zoom with two people who work for her and another long phone call. That’s when she said things like, “This part, really? Do we have to?” And I’d say, “We do.” What was she most upset about? The number one thing was the way I wrote about her father. She kept saying, “There’s just a tone.” And when I looked again, I thought, “You know what? She’s right.” It was a little snarky. He’s been dead for so long that he had stopped feeling like a real person to me. To her, he’s still alive in her mind. She also thought the sex tape material went on too long, and the Damon Thomas [Kardashian’s first husband] material made her squirm. But she read a couple of other chapters [about her earlier years] and cried because they were so true to her experience as a 13-year-old. She said it made her give that little girl some grace. In the end, she accepted the material she had objected to. I cut two sentences for her because they concerned her safety. “She wanted to be famous so badly, she got exactly what she wanted, and she loves it.” Jonathan Van Meter, on Kardashian (pictured in ninth grade) @kimkardashian/Instagram. Has her family read it? A couple of months ago, Kim called me late at night. She’d been at Khloé’s house, where Khloé told her Kris had flipped out on camera while they were filming the show. She was yelling, “Why did Kim drag us all into this? Why is my affair from 30 years ago in the book?” Two days later, Kris was fine. But it’s going to be on the show. Kim said to her mother: “All this stuff gets written about us, and then a guy comes along who gets us and wants to explain us. Why wouldn’t you want that?” That’s the closest I got to an answer about why she did the book. So why did she take that risk in the first place? Was she looking for legitimacy? I think that’s the simplest answer. She’d been written about for years through scandal and gossip, and here was somebody who wanted to really explain her. But in 2020, that felt more urgent than it does now. People increasingly understand that her criminal justice work is real, that she studied law seriously. There are still people who hear you’re writing a biography of Kim Kardashian and look at you as though you’ve lost your mind. It’s in the first line of the book: You can tell a lot about a person when you say you’re writing a book about Kim Kardashian. She has documented so much of her own life already. What could you discover that wasn’t already splashed across television or Instagram? Her life is so self-mediated. Nobody had really told it from a writer’s perspective. She understood that: “I know this book is from your point of view. It’s your book.” The challenge was vulnerability. Her childhood friends said she never showed it, even as a little girl. You couldn’t tell how she felt about difficult things. What she did intuit was how journalism works. Most people outside the business don’t understand the difference between “off the record” and “on background.” Kim did. She’d say, “I’ll tell you this whole weird, crazy, dark story, and then we can decide what words I want to come out of my mouth. I want you to know it and I want you to write about it, but I don’t want it coming from me.” It took until the summer of 2024, when I spent time with her in Malibu, before she really cracked open. What changed in Malibu? The visits were open-ended, and she was alone. Before that, I’d interview her while she worked out, or she’d call while getting her hair dyed. We’d talk at photo shoots, with a whole glam squad around. I estimate we spent something like 50 hours together going back to 2019. She could be completely open, but there was a boundary. In Malibu, it was just, “Come over.” We’d hang out in the living room. Most of the time she was in sweats, without makeup. Once she had just had a needling procedure and her face was bruised. Another time she came down the staircase in this gold outfit, fully made up, from a child’s dinosaur-themed birthday party. I asked what she was dressed as. She said, “Cleopatra.” Tell me about your first real dinner together. Casa Vega, in the Valley. She drove herself up in a Range Rover, wearing a full-length black leather coat and boots. We sat down, and she was just like every other girl. She ordered a strawberry daiquiri, took three sips, and I asked if I could finish it. Then she noticed girls at another table filming her. They eventually approached us, pretty aggressively. She handled it like a pro. I was struck by how normal she could be in a situation that was completely abnormal. Paris HIlton and Kardashian in 2006. Van Meter noted that Hilton canceled their interview 17 times over about four months: “Eventually I thought the cancellations were more interesting than whatever she’d tell me. Kim was so mad when I told her. It seemed to stir up some ancient irritation between them. The creation turning on the creator.” Chris Polk/Filmmagic For Bragman Nyman Cafarelli You also saw her deal with her daughter North when she was upset. There was a Vogue shoot, and North had imagined that she and Kim would wear matching dresses. When they didn’t, she had a meltdown. Kim took her away. Later she told me they’d laid on the bed together for about 15 minutes without talking. She just held her until she calmed down, then explained things to her. I remember thinking, “My mother never did that for me.” It made me feel Kim trusted me with something parents don’t necessarily want outsiders to see. I know you grew up in relatively modest circumstances in Atlantic City. Were you surprised by the scale of Kim’s life? I walked into her house one day and saw a woman mopping floors way off in the distance. It reminded me of The Crown , where you occasionally see somebody vacuuming Buckingham Palace. There’s always somebody cleaning, a chef, nannies, assistants. But I never felt the grossness I’ve sometimes felt around very rich people. It felt warm. At the same time, there are gates into Hidden Hills and then another gate and armed security. It’s a bubble. How much of the apparent domestic normalcy survives the machinery around her? Both things exist. You go through a gate into Hidden Hills, then through another gate at her house, and there’s armed security. But the family lives nearby, and the kids ride their bikes between houses. In Malibu, she told me she bought the house next door so the employees could work and park over there. She was trying to get the chaos out of her home. And there were odd, unguarded moments. At a photo shoot, I looked up from my phone and she was completely naked while people helped her change. Neither of us flinched. At another shoot, she was texting like a chainsaw, but she still heard every word of the conversation happening around her. You watched her work up close. How much of the business is actually Kim and how much is the team around her? I went to see her one day when she was shooting two back-to-back covers — one of them was Vogue Hong Kong. We were in the glam room, and she was directing everything: the air-conditioning, the music, the makeup. And at the same time, she was on the phone with Tyra Banks, trying to persuade her to appear in a Skims campaign with other supermodels. Tyra was feeling insecure. Kim spent hours lovingly talking her into it. I thought, “That’s Anna Wintour plus an advertising agency plus the model in the shoot.” She was wearing seven hats at once. Skims isn’t just underwear. It’s a platform and a fashion company and a very strange conglomeration of things. It’s also an empire that was launched by a sex tape. How do you think that happened? Do you see her as someone exploited by a humiliating episode or someone who brilliantly capitalized on it? Both. I think she was humiliated by it and at some point decided to capitalize on something beyond her control. We talked about its effect on her life almost from the beginning. But she can’t really talk about exactly how it happened. Ray J and Kim were together for years, filming all kinds of things, including sex. Somehow footage ended up with Vivid. I don’t know how that happened, and Kim is never going to tell. Ray J has claimed that Kris Jenner was involved in arranging its release. If that turned out to be true, wouldn’t it change your understanding of their entire origin story? No, it wouldn’t! And I still don’t believe Kris had anything to do with it. But you didn’t interview Ray J. No. Nor Kanye West, arguably the most important creative influence on her transformation into a fashion icon. Wasn’t that a significant hole in your reporting? Kim initially said, “Of course he’s going to talk to you.” But as his behavior grew more troubling, I didn’t think it would be ethical to interview somebody in the middle of a mental health crisis. Years ago, I profiled someone who was high out of her mind, and I thought, “This is like date rape. There’s no consent here.” I promised myself I’d never let that happen again. When he tipped into raging antisemitism, I thought it might ruin the book. He was central to her life, and suddenly he was a pariah. But Kim managed to separate herself from that, and in a way his absence kept the focus on her story. Later someone said that if you get him on the phone, he’ll talk for seven hours. I didn’t need seven hours straight from Kanye West. Was there anyone who turned you down? Paris Hilton. Late in the process, I told Kim I should talk to her. Kim checked and said Paris agreed, but I had to go through her publicist. That was unusual: With everybody else, Kim just sent a text. I sent questions, connected with Paris’ assistant, and then the interview was canceled 17 times over about four months. Eventually I thought the cancellations were more interesting than whatever she’d tell me. Kim was so mad when I told her. It seemed to stir up some ancient irritation between them. The creation turning on the creator. What did the interviews with her sisters reveal to you about the family? Kourtney took about nine months to talk to me. At one point, her assistant asked if we could do it while they filmed the show, which I didn’t think Kim would appreciate. Khloé jumped right in. Kim told her she didn’t have to get glammed up, and of course she got fully glammed up. I became convinced that what you see on the show is mostly real. Kim and Kourtney can be wicked to each other. Kim and Khloé are genuinely close. Kendall and Kylie are so much younger that Kim has almost maternal pride in them. She once said to me, “My mom made all of her mistakes on me.” By the time she got to Kylie, she’d perfected it. I know you spent a whole lot of time with their grandmother MJ. She was one of the warmest people I’ve ever met. She told me the history of the maternal side of the family going back to Arkansas. Again and again these women would divorce a shitty man and open a store. Kim’s mother is Kris, Kris’ mother is MJ, and before that there was Lou Ethel and Tiny. You begin to see a family history of women making their own way. So who’s the head matriarch now — Kris or Kim? It’s already shifting to Kim. In Malibu in 2024, she said to me, “I’m the one who pushes everybody. It’s me. It’s not my mom.” Did the family help you understand her or did they mostly reinforce the version of themselves we already know? I first spent time with the family years earlier when I profiled Kendall. We drove around Calabasas and Hidden Hills, played miniature golf and ran out of gas. Kris cooked dinner one night. I asked where I could have a cigarette, and she said, “Come with me.” We picked up our vodka drinks and smoked by the pool. I thought, “I love this woman.” That experience made me receptive to Kim before I really knew her. It was the opposite of what people assume about the family. Doesn’t that suggest you’d already lost some journalistic distance even before you started the book? Maybe. But I was also trying to get past a kind of reflexive contempt. When the book was announced, people would visibly recoil. Some people simply don’t want any serious analysis of Kim. But you don’t have to like her to recognize her enormous effect on the culture. Anna Wintour blurbed your book. When Vogue first put Kim on the cover, readers canceled their subscriptions. What finally brought Anna around? Probably some combination of Kanye’s relentless campaign, realizing that magazines were in trouble and that people like Kim had millions of followers, and recognizing that the world was changing. Hollywood got Kim sooner. They could see that Kris and Kim are powerful and make money. But people like Graydon Carter and Maureen Dowd thought it was nonsense. Every time Maureen Dowd dropped Kim’s name into her column without actually writing about her, I thought, “What are you doing?” It felt like using her for clicks. But Kim doesn’t care. It just doesn’t mean anything to her. The subtitle calls Kim “The Woman Who Created the Future.” What does that mean? That subtitle was suggested to me, and at first I said, “That’s not right.” Then weeks went by, and I thought, “Actually, hmm.” As a teenager, she was selling things on eBay before anybody had heard of eBay. She had a blog with members — essentially followers — and posted videos of herself talking about dating. She was an early adopter of every single one of these things. People only look at what happened after 2007. Everything before she was famous was the stuff I cared about most. Isn’t that also a future of relentless materialism and everyone making themselves the center of the universe? Isn’t that what people don’t like about her? Yes, but I don’t

title: Jonathan Groff to Return to Broadway in Solo Play ‘The Amish Project’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jonathan Groff attends The 78th Annual Tony Awards at Radio City Music Hall on June 08, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images) Michael Loccisano/Getty Images Jonathan Groff is returning to Broadway this season in the solo play The Amish Project. The play, written by Jessica Dickey, is a fictional exploration of a schoolhouse shooting in an Amish community, and how the community learns to provide forgiveness and compassion. Sarna Lapine will direct the show, which is slated to begin performances Feb. 10, 2027, at the Broadhurst Theatre. The play debuted at the New York International Fringe Festival and was developed at the Cherry Lane Theatre before premiering Off-Broadway at the Rattlestick Playwrights Theater in 2009. It has since had productions at regional theaters across the U.S. and around the world. The play is typically performed as a one-woman show, with the main actor playing multiple characters. Groff will perform the play as written. Related Stories Lifestyle Tom Hanks Sets Broadway Return in 'This World of Tomorrow' Lifestyle Daniel Kaluuya to Make U.S. Stage Debut in New Branden Jacobs-Jenkins Play This marks the third Broadway project for Groff in recent years, following his Tony-nominated run in Just In Time from March 2025 to 2026 and his Tony-winning role in Merrily We Roll Along in the 2023-2024 season . He comes to the project after making his Royal Shakespeare Company debut in As You Like It this past fall. He recently completed production on Lin-Manuel Miranda’s feature adaptation of Octet , as well as the independent film Trust the Man , which he stars in opposite Daniel Radcliffe. The subject matter of the play struck a chord with Groff, who grew up nearby in Amish country. “20 years ago this month, an unimaginable tragedy happened in a one room Amish schoolhouse in Lancaster, Pennsylvania and Jessica Dickey wrote an astounding work of art in response. Sarna Lapine sent me The Amish Project last year and I was floored by the urgency and potent poetry of Jessica’s writing as she dives headfirst into the many aftershocks of this horrific event and explores the idea that sometimes the most radical human act is forgiveness. I am profoundly grateful to be bringing Jessica’s play to Broadway alongside Sarna and this incredible team,” Groff said. Robert Ahrens and Tom Kirdahy, producers of Just In Time , are producing the play. THR

title: Judge Orders Trump to Testify Under Oath in BBC Defamation Lawsuit
full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 23, 2026 1:55am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Donald Trump at a midterm rally in Kansas, Oct. 19, 2026. Courtesy of Getty Logo text A U.S. judge has told Donald Trump that he must answer questions in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC or face sanctions. If the President does not sit for a deposition under oath by Dec. 11, the most extreme outcome might include the dismissal of the entire suit, according to the BBC . Last year, Trump sued the British broadcaster over claims that a BBC Panorama documentary was doctored to make it appear as though Trump, during his Jan. 6, 2021 speech outside the White House, had urged his followers to attack the Capitol. Related Stories Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title TV 'MobLand' EP Teases What Season 3 Holds for Tom Hardy as 'Laird' Star Peter Sarsgaard Shares How He Feels About Playing a "Malevolent U.S. Billionaire" The 33-page document, brought in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida last December, alleges that the BBC made “a false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory, and malicious depiction of President Trump.” A BBC spokesperson told The Hollywood Reporter as news of the lawsuit broke: “While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree [that] there is a basis for a defamation claim.” Ten months later, Trump cancelled a previous deposition set for Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” A lawyer for the BBC said in court that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia and had “prioritized that” over answering questions. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by Dec. 11 or he’ll face sanctions, unless this “discovery period” — described by the BBC as the phase where both sides provide internal or other records that could form evidence — is extended. All of this came about when a leaked BBC memo from an independent advisor, a man named Michael Prescott, concluded that the doc Trump: A Second Chance? “seemed to be taking a distinctly anti-Trump stance.” In the speech, Trump said: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women.” However, in the Panorama edit, he was shown saying: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol … and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” The two clips stitched together were, in actuality, more than 50 minutes apart. THR

Discussions will explore IP monetization, global franchise expansion and emerging business models driven by AI, digital platforms and evolving investment strategies. U.S. participants include The Raine Group; Shamrock Capital; Atwater Capital; J.P. Morgan Global Corporate Bank; Amblin Entertainment; and Anonymous Content, who all bring perspectives across entertainment finance, investment and production. title: ‘Apart,’ Set in Cyprus and Apartheid South Africa, “Challenges the Idea of ‘Us’ and ‘Them'” (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 23, 2026 1:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Apart' Courtesy of PÖFF Can a young woman forced to leave a divided Cyprus in the 1970s find belonging and even love in an arranged marriage in Apartheid South Africa, especially when a secret from her past threatens to change everything? With Apart , South African Cypriot writer-director Stelana Kliris ( Find Me Falling , Committed ) has created a deeply personal film about displacement, belonging, borders, both the ones that are physical and those that are in our hearts, and human connections. And it is inspired by the real experiences of her refugee parents. The movie, world-premiering at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), stars Leem Lubany ( Omar , Rock the Kasbah ), Luca Pasqualino ( Rivals , The Musketeers ) and Girley Jazama ( Under the Hanging Tree , The White Line ). Related Stories Movies 'Biermann' Director Explains Why His Doc About a German Political Singer Is a Film for the Trump Era Business Nobody Knew This Game Existed, and Now It's a Hot 2027 Title “In 1974, when Turkey invades Cyprus, young Eleni (Lubany) leaves her homeland through an arranged marriage and finds herself in Apartheid South Africa, swapping one divided country for another,” reads a synopsis for the film. “There, a new life with Nico (Pasqualino) slowly turns into love, until an unexpected friendship forces her to confront a secret from her past.” Shot in Cyprus with a story that goes between Cyprus and South Africa, Apart brings a turbulent time in the 1970s to life, with a focus on a female perspective. The filmmaker’s Find Me Falling became the first Cypriot film to premiere on Netflix. Apart will open Tallinn’s Critics’ Picks section. “With this very personal and ambitious film, Stelana Kliris has delivered a deeply moving cinematic ode to humanity, a film that will stay with you long after the final frame,” the festival website teases. With cinematography by Simon Sarketzis and editing by Emilios Avraam, Apart is being sold by Reinvent Yellow Sales. The producers are Kliris, Susan Simnett, Jamie Harvey and Ioanna Bolomyti. “It has always fascinated me that people like my parents, who emigrated from Cyprus to South Africa, left one divided place for another, and I wanted to translate this into a film that challenges the idea of ‘us’ and ‘them,’ and, whilst the central narrative is fictional, the individual events around it are from real events,” Kliris says. “This is an intimate, character-driven film with a specific set of aesthetics that represents not just the two locations, but two distinct periods, 1970s South Africa interwoven with flashbacks to the Cypriot past, and while war and Apartheid serve as the backdrop, our story of love, friendship and identity provides for a more human, intimate experience.” THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for Apart . Prepare for a touching journey through time and across the globe to get a first glimpse of the challenges and emotions the protagonists experience. THR

title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: Peter Berg’s Powerful True WWII Story Takes Four Star Players From The Glory Of The Football Field To The Hell Of The Battlefield – AFI Fest
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgård Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Review: Sacha Baron Cohen’s Signature Prankster Returns In Outrageous Form With Something To Offend Everyone AFI Fest Opens Tonight: President & CEO Bob Gazzale On Why It Matters In The Oscar-Season Deluge Of Film Festivals – The Deadline Interview View All October 23, 2026 12:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source The Mosquito Bowl Netflix There have been so many films about WWII, both during and after, so many different takes and personal stories told, that now 81 years since it ended it is hard to imagine finding a fresh way to say anything new, but with his film adaptation of Buzz Bissinger’s best seller, The Mosquito Bowl : A Game Of Life And Death In World War II , filmmaker Peter Berg has done just that with a powerful and ultimately poignant portrait focusing on four very young star college football players who enlist after the bombing of Pearl Harbor and go on to fight the bruising Battle Of Okinawa. In less than three months they go from a football field to a very different battlefield where the score is sadly measured in lives lost, not points won. Related Stories News Jenna Ortega Plans To "Be Off The TV For A While" After 'Wednesday' Casting 'The Watcher' Season 2 Adds Madelaine Petsch, Evan Adams, Owen Painter & Quintessa Swindell The team of Berg and Bissinger seems appropriate here since both gave us that classic of Texas football, Friday Night Lights, and now find a new uniquely moving connection to the sport and the young men who played it. In the Netflix film, The Mosquito Bowl, which had its World Premiere Thursday night at AFI Fest in Hollywood, this true story of the transition of young star players who signed up to serve their country in its darkest hour becomes one of the most effective anti-war films I have ever seen, one that never resorts to preaching or false patriotic rah-rah posturing. Watch on Deadline It achieves its true strength by putting us directly into the center of the hell of war, a visceral experience so intense and unrelenting it seems we are there and, like those who were on the front lines, a feeling there is no way out. Make no mistake, despite the premise, this is not a football movie, it is a war movie putting us right in harms way into the thick of battle, a film about the unforgiving nature of combat, and in that way makes you think twice about the price of it all and, 86 years later, about the cost now of wars being waged that never should have been started. Ultimately this is a human story, but fair warning, Berg whose films have included Lone Survivor, Deep Water Horizon, and other tales of valor and courage against all odds, does not hold back in showing the true horrors of the fight, in this case a noble one. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, four of America’s greatest college football stars — John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), Tony Butkovich ( Ray Nicholson ) and David Schreiner ( Tom Francis ), in their late teens or early twenties put country over fame and enlist in the Marines. They were like others who experience glory in sports who had to face a nightmare, a violent unforgiving battlefield for which they had little time to prepare. Berg’s screenplay, written with Mark L. Smith introduces us to four men, putting the focus on them to tell a larger story. We move from 1941 college ball to training at Parris Island in South Carolina, right into the front lines in the Pacific Theater. The story is essentially told through the eyes of Galitzine’s McLaughry, an impressive young man with deep talents that will take him far in life if he can survive a war with no timetable for its end. Each of the others we follow along the way are distinctive personalities, with Nicholson’s vibrant Tony Butkovich a massive star player you feel could withstand hits from any direction; Skarsgard’s Bob Bauman a little more loose with a devil-may-care attitude; and Francis’ Scheiner a more shy and humble type of All American. In the telling of this particular tale in WWII these four represent many others, but it is smart of Berg and Bissinger to zero in on just a few, because in addition to all the shooting and explosions and sounds and sights of carnage all around them, we have time to see their humanity, their fortitude, and heroism, their bonding, all of which makes the inevitable loss of young lives all that much more emotional. The bulk of this film is war, but as it was for 64 college players who gathered one afternoon , there is a brief respite from it all in the Mosquito Bowl, an organized game that would take them back to earlier times. For a moment they were all boys again, superstar players, tossing the ball, hitting the end zone. It wasn’t just relief for them, it is also for the audience now watching it unfold because it shows how time was fleeting. What is to come afterwards is when their world is on fire as the fierce Battle Of Okinawa Island takes them , and us, back to sad reality. In actual numbers 14 of the young men playing that game that day would die on Okinawa, three of them were among the four Marines we get to know so well. In terms of filmmaking this is one of Berg’s most impressive outings. He shot in sequence, not the usual course in production, and it clearly helped the actors build their brotherhood and camraderie in authentic fashion. The use of tight camera lens and handheld against a 360 degree background that takes in the whole environment the characters are experiencing is very effectively employed. Thanks to the exceptional cinematography of Jacques Jouffret we are right in their faces. Shout out also to editors Jon Otazua and Garret Donnelly, as well as the music score from Explosions In The Sky, a regular contributor to Berg’s films. The four main stars, Galitzine, Skarsgard, Nicholson, and Francis are completely believable as football stars suddenly thrust into the life of a Marine with little time to train before being shipped out knowing it might be a one way ticket. It is a fine ensemble in a movie well worth seeing not as just another war movie but rather one that should make any leader think hard about the human price paid everytime they start one. Producers are Berg, Brian Grazer, and Alex Gayner. full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Meghan Markle “Deeply Distressed” Over Allegation Her Father Possessed Child Abuse Images Prince William Says He’s A Christopher Nolan & ‘The Celebrity Traitors’ Super Fan ‘Enola Holmes’ Star Louis Partridge To Headline & Produce Film ‘One Last Summer’ View All October 23, 2026 12:05am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Louis Partridge Keith Kandell EXCLUSIVE : Louis Partridge , the English actor best known for Enola Holmes and House of Guinness , will star in and produce the coming-of-age indie film One Last Summer . Partridge will be joined by Mia Jenkins ( Love Me Love Me , Geek Girl ) and Jude Carmichael ( Dear England at The National Theatre), with further cast to be announced. Written and directed by Misha Citron, whose credits include Enola Holmes, filming on One Last Summer wrapped in Tuscany, Italy. Partridge and Citron have co-founded Pipe Dream Films, which housed the One Last Summe r production. Related Stories News Louis Partridge & Anson Boon Set For British Coming-Of-Age Film 'Andy & Orson'; MetFilm Launches Sales For TIFF Market News Mckenna Grace, Paul Walter Hauser & Louis Partridge To Star In Rom-Com 'The Official Mistress' About Final Days Of The French Monarchy - Cannes Market Here’s the logline: “Set over a weekend in the Tuscan countryside, One Last Summer follows Milo (Partridge), who returns to the house of his late, estranged father with his best friend Zac (Carmichael). Watch on Deadline “Milo is convinced into a double date with two American travellers that starts strong but sharply unravels. Each character must reckon with their past selves, who they are now, and what they’re leaving behind in Italy. The film captures the intensity of brief relationships in youth.” Jim Parks, producer of Steven Soderbergh’s The Christophers , produces alongside Maya Nurmohamed and Saskia Steinberg of Blue Lobster Productions. Partridge said: “As an actor and a first-time producer, I loved leaning into true creative collaboration. Our aim being to make the film for ourselves, as young people to enjoy first and foremost. In doing so we hope to create something simultaneously specific and with universal scope.” Citron added: “I wanted to create a dynamic between the ensemble that reflected the charge and intimacy of youth, feeling the sweetness of attraction that is cruelly muddied by inevitable insecurity, fear, and, often unfortunately at this age, grief.” Partridge is repped by Independent Talent Group and WME. Jenkins is repped by Alexander Cooke at B-Side Management & Alissa Vradenburg at Untitled Entertainment. full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Jon Tower Named Permanent Executive Producer Of ‘CBS Mornings’ Politico Corrects Susie Wiles Story After Trump Official’s Threat, But Media Outlet’s Attorney Warns White House Of “Unconstitutional Retaliation” White House Correspondents’ Association Decries Trump Team’s “Retaliation” After POTUS Lashes Out At Reporter View All March 5, 2026 6:14am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R) Former 'CBS Mornings' co-anchor Tony Dokoupil, Shawna Thomas, Gayle King and Nate Burleson Photo by Michele Crowe/CBS via Getty Images Shawna Thomas is departing as executive producer of CBS Mornings , as the show has been expected to get an overhaul under the network’s new owners Paramount Skydance. A network spokesperson confirmed Thomas’ departure, which was first reported by Variety . Thomas has served as EP since 2021. Related Stories News Gayle King Will Stay At ‘CBS Mornings’ As She Renews Deal With Network News Tony Dokoupil Asserts ‘CBS Evening News’ Will Be Independent From Its Corporate Owner: “I Report For You” “For five years, I’ve tried to make this show something she and everybody on this team want to be a part of. Want to watch. Want to learn from,” Thomas wrote in a note to staffers. She wrote that she had been “thinking about this for a while and, frankly, I’m tired y’all.” Jon Tower will run CBS Mornings on an interim basis after Thomas departs at the end of the month, wrote Tom Cibrowski, president and executive editor of CBS News . Watch on Deadline Cibrowski wrote, “Morning television moves fast. It demands grace under pressure, sharp instincts, and the ability to pivot at a moment’s notice. Shawna does all of that with a calm confidence and a great sense of humor. Morning television is also a tight-knit family. Behind the scenes, Shawna’s leadership creates space for collaboration, creativity, and trust – and on screen, that translates into something viewers can feel.” The news of Thomas’ departure comes a day after the announcement that Gayle King renewed her deal to remain as co-host and at the network. Executives also indicated that co-host Nate Burleson would remain, while the show’s traditional slot for a third co-host has been vacant since Tony Dokoupil departed to become anchor of CBS Evening News . CBS Mornings averaged 1.9 million viewers in the fourth quarter of last year, behind NBC’s Today with 2.9 million and ABC’s Good Morning America with 2.7 million, according to Nielsen. During Thomas’ tenure, the show underwent a revamp, with a new title from CBS This Morning , while taking on some of the elements of the network’s long-running Sunday Morning . It has distinguished itself as a newsier rival to Today and Good Morning America , and Thomas came with a hard news background, having served as Washington bureau chief for Vice News and, before that, working for NBC News for more than a decade. Thomas wrote that the CBS Mornings team “has made me more thoughtful, empathetic and expanded my personal definition of storytelling. I’ve had the privilege of helping to make 10 (now 12!) hours of television each week that goes out free to people everywhere. I’ve taken that responsibility of trying to inform, educate, entertain and make people care about the world around them very seriously, and I know the people here do, too.” ‘Top Gun’, ‘Picket Fences’ And ‘Alien’ Star Dies At 93; Career In Photos ‘Clayface’ Solid $3.5M Thursday Previews; Can He Scare Off Elizabeth Holmes?
